Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m.
Karakia.
Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON (Minister for Treaty of Waitangi
Negotiations) on behalf of the Leader of the House: In the absence of both the Leader
of the House and the Deputy Leader of the Ho use, I am required to read this statement
to the House. I do apologise. I have not had time to memorise it. When the House
resumes on Tuesday, 31 July—[ Interruption] never call me petulant—the Government
will look to progress the Committee stage of  the Biosecurity Law Reform Bill, the
Juries (Jury Service and Protec tion of Particulars of Jury List Information) Amendment
Bill, the Commerce Commission (Internatio nal Co-operation, and Fees) Bill, the
Sentencing (Aggravating Factors) Amen dment Bill, and the Appropriation (2012/13
Estimates) Bill.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I call the honourable shadow Lead er of the House, who will not
need to read it at all.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: In the absence of my friend
and colleague Russel Norman, I will not read a response.
Infrastructure Investment Programme—Progress
1. Dr CAM CALDER (National)  to the Minister of Finance: What progress is the
Government making with its multi-billion dollar infrastructure programme?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Our progress on infrastructure is
good. We have invested $5 billion in infras tructure such as schools, broadband, and
hospitals over the last four Budgets, and billions more upgrading our State highway
networks and the national grid. The first road of national significance project, Victoria
Park Tunnel, has been completed and th ere is good progress on the rest. We have
upgraded on average over 16,000 State houses  a year since 2009, a nd are on track to
insulate every State house built before 1978 by the end of the year. Of course, we have
put aside $5.5 billion to help fund the rebuild of Christchurch infrastructure, which is
getting under way.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: What steps has the Government ta ken to improve the quality of its
infrastructure investment?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, that is a good question, because just having more
infrastructure is one aspect of it, but having high-quality infrastructure is, in the long
run, more important. We have improved the way the Government makes its own plans
and the way it gets consents and finances its infrastructure through the reform of the
Resource Management Act, setting up the Na tional Infrastructure Unit, and setting up
the Environmental Protection Authority. This has introduced more discipline into the
Government process. Last year we issued  the second National Infrastructure Plan,
which shows that our infrastr ucture is generally improving, but it does highlight those
areas where we need to do a better job.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: How will the Government fund its large infrastructure investment?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The planned investment over th e next 4 years is large, at
around $17 billion. This will be paid for thr ough a mixture of funding sources. Some of
it, of course, will come from petrol tax and road-user charges on the roads, some will
4010 Questions for Oral Answer 26 Jul 2012
come from depreciation, and a considerable amount will come from direct funding from
the Government. The direct funding from the Government will be channelled through
the Future Investment Fund, which was set up to  take the proceeds of the partial share
sales and invest those in future publicly owned infrastructure. Treasury is forecasting
sale proceeds of $5 billion to $7 billion over th e next 3 to 5 years, and this will assist
with a $17 billion infrastructure investment programme.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Does he agree with the 52 percent of business leaders in the
New Zealand Herald ’s “Mood of the Boardroom” survey that other than returning to
surplus, the Government has no adequate pl an to encourage the economic growth and
jobs needed to stop so many young New Zealanders moving to Australia?

items.speaker: Hon Steven Joyce
items.text: Oh, so not enough plans today? So we have changed from too
many plans again.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, I do not, and as my colleague Steven Joyce has pointed
out, the Labour Party cannot decide—on some days there are too many plans, and on
the other days there is no plan. We have outlined the programme, outlined the plan,
including to the “Mood of the Boardroom” se ssion this morning. I can tell the member
that it has pretty broad support among the business community.
Overseas Investment Rules—2010 Sale of Crafar Farms to Natural Dairy
2. RICHARD PROSSER (NZ First)  to the Minister for Land Information : Can
the public have confidence that the Overseas Investment Office is taking prompt action
in relation to all breaches of the Overseas Investment Act 2005; if so, how?

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.role: Actin g Minister for Land Information

items.text: Yes. The Overseas Investment Office promp tly investigates all suspected breaches of
the Overseas Investment Act 2005. I have some good news for that honourable member:
in the period 1 July 2011 to 30 June 2012, 100 percent—100 percen t—of public alerts
about potential breaches were  assessed for possible invest igation within 10 working
days.

items.speaker: Richard Prosser
items.text: Given that answer, will he tell the House what action the Overseas
Investment Office has taken in respect of th e four Crafar farms sold to an overseas
investor without consent; or, alternatively, will he explain why no action has been
taken?

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: I do not have particular information about
particular applications or particular concerns to hand. If the member wants an answer to
a particular question, I suggest he either ask it as the primar y question or put it down as
a written question to the Minister.

items.speaker: Richard Prosser
items.text: How can the public have confidence in the Overseas Investment
Office when UBNZ Assets Holdings, a co mpany associated with May Wang, who
failed a good-character test, was able to pur chase four of the Crafar farms without
permission and get away with it?

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: The same principle applies: if the member
wants direct answers to speci fic questions, he should eith er ask them as a primary
question or put them down as a written question.

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Did we not determine a
number of weeks ago that if  a Minister did not know the answer, the Minister should
simply say that they do not know the answer?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Well, I think the Minister basically said that, but he was a little
more helpful in suggesting that maybe if  members want detailed information in
answers, they need to make it clear in th e primary question what they are asking. I do
not think the Minister was being unhelpful.
26 Jul 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 4011
New Zealand - Australia Migration—18 to 30 Age Range
3. Hon DAVID PARKER (Labour)  to the Minister of Finance: Does he stand by
his statement regarding migration to Austra lia “What’s the point of standing in the
airport crying about it?”; if so, how many of the 53,763 people that migrated to
Australia in the year to June 2012 are from 18 to 30 years of age in number and
percentage terms?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes; and, as I said in the rest of that
statement, we have just got to compete. New Zealand should show the aspiration and
confidence that it can compete with a la rger, more wealthy economy for our young
people’s talent, instead of just worrying about it. So 21,585 people aged 18 to 30
migrated to Australia in the year to June 2012—about 40 percent of the total. I note that
in the 9 years to June 2008, when economic conditions were more benign, 305,800 New
Zealanders left for Australia, and around 36 percent of them were aged 18 to 30.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Does he agree with the findings of the New Zealand Herald
“Mood of the Boardroom” survey, which found that out of eight critical issues his
Government has performed worst on stemming the outward flow of Kiwis?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, and as I suggested to the large group of business leaders
in the room, it is up to them to compete for that talent by showing the leadership and the
opportunities to our young New Zealanders. If they are waiting around for someone to
do that on their behalf, then they can rely on this Government to create positive
conditions, but it is in the workplaces of New Zealand th at young people will see the
opportunities that attract them. It is time we showed the confidence that we can compete
with Australia.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Does he think it is sustaina ble to lose 21,000 people per annum
to Australia—the equivalent of the en tire student body of Otago or Victoria
universities?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I do not think that is going to  continue, because the relative
economic performance of New Zealand and Aust ralia is starting to close the gap. If we
persist with the Government ’s broad-based economic programme to create jobs and
opportunities, and fix problems like housing affordability, then we will be able to
compete with Australia for our young talent. That is better than telling our young people
that the Government is going to waste more of their money, borrow more, and not
support the businesses that provide their jobs—which is Labour’s policy.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: When he said yesterday that migration rates are correlated to
growth rates, does the fact that New Zeala nd experienced the highest number ever of
people migrating to Australia in a 12-month pe riod signify that he has failed in his goal
of growing the New Zealand economy, and in stead is growing the Australian economy
by sending 20,000 young New Zealanders there a year?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, what it signifies is that  Australia has had a once-in-a-
100-year increase in its income because of  its coal and iron-ore boom. That gave
Australia higher growth rates—for a short time—than New Zealand’s. We would expect
that, as our own programme starts to have a positive impact on the New Zealand
economy, those flows will change.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Given that young people are leav ing in droves to Australia,
what plans does he have to ensure the l ong-term sustainability of superannuation, given
the changing age profile, particularly in light of the fact that 88 percent of the chief
executive officers in the “Mood of the Bo ardroom” survey said that National is
completely on the wrong side and out to lunch on the issue of raising the age of
eligibility for superannuation?
4012 Questions for Oral Answer 26 Jul 2012

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The most important thing for New Zealand superannuation
is a thriving economy. If we do not have  a thriving economy, then in the future
superannuitants will not have adequate supe rannuation. That is why we are focusing on
encouraging businesses to i nvest and employ. We are fo cusing on using our natural
resources, through oil and gas exploration and mining, and on supporting our primary
industries, so they can be more compe titive on the global stage—all of which are
policies that the Opposition oppose.
Child Poverty—Effect on Māori Children
4. METIRIA TUREI (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Minister of M āori Affairs: Ka
whakaae a ia ki t ā te Kaik ōmihana Whanaungata ā-Iwi, a Joris De Bres, i k ī rā, “Many
Māori children are being denied their ba sic human rights because of poverty and
inadequate public services”?
[Does he agree with Race Relations Commi ssioner Joris De Bres that “Many M āori
children are being denied their basic human rights because of po verty and inadequate
public services”?]

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: T ēnā koe kai te
Kaiwhakawā. Tēnā koe Metiria i pātai mai i tēnā pātai, he pātai nui tēnei te pōharatanga
e pā ana ki ā tātau iwi. Anei r ā tāku—ahakoa ko wai te tangata, he pakeke, he tamaiti
rānei, mehemea ka noho pōhara, ka noho ia i te kore mana.
[Thank you, Mr Speaker, and to you, Metiri a, who asked that question, which is an
important one about this poverty that affect s our people. This poverty relating to our
people is a big one. My view on it is that it does not matt er who the person is, an adult
or a child, when one is impoverished, one loses status.]

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. In the translation—and I
think, in fact, directly—the Minister breach ed Standing Orders in the way that he
addressed a member of the House. I think it is important, even when one is speaking in
Māori, that the same standards apply.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I hear what the member is saying, but I do not believe that it was
intentionally unfair or unkind. I think the member wa s actually acknowledging a fellow
colleague in a warm way, and I would not like to interfere in that, although I accept the
member’s point that we should refer to all members by their full names. But on this
occasion I would not like to interfere, b ecause I do not think the member involved took
offence, anyway, at being referred to in that manner.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Thank you, Lockwood.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does the Minister consider it acceptable that one-third of all M āori
children live in poverty, and th at the Government has failed to address inequality,
thereby condemning these M āori children to a life of sickness, hardship, and
underachievement?

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: Ā, e maha atu ngā tamariki e noho pōhara ana. Kāre au
e tautoko ana ki t ēnā. Nā reira n ā tēnā, nā te tono o te P āti Māori kua whakat ūria e te
Kāwanatanga tētahi komiti, kia titiro ki ēnei mea te p ōharatanga kei roto i te iwi. Ko te
Prime Minister Tuarua te heamana, ā, ko Tariana Turia te heamana tuarua. Atu ki tēnā, i
raro i taku mahi m ō Te Puni K ōkiri, me te mahi o Wh ānau Ora, he maha ng ā ūmanga
kua whakatūria e mātau, kia whakamāmā ai te pōharatanga kei roto i tō tātau iwi.
[There are many children living in poverty, and I do not agree with that. Because of
that and the request by the M āori Party, Government established a committee to look at
these things that affect poverty in our people. The Deputy Prime Minister is the chair
and Tariana Turia is the deputy chair. Beyond that and through my work with Te Puni
26 Jul 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 4013
Kōkiri and the role of Wh ānau Ora, many enterprises have been established to ease
poverty amongst our people.]

items.speaker: Hon Nanaia Mahuta
items.text: He aha te whakatau o te Minita kia taea ng ā whānau M āori
me ā rātau tamariki he pūtea oranga inā, e noho ana tētahi hautoru Māori i te pōhara me
te rawakore, me te tokomaha o ng ā tamariki e haumaru ana i te matua kotahi? He aha
ngā kaupapa pai mō ēnei tamariki ki ngā kura auraki?
[What decision has the Minister come to that will enable M āori families and their
children to receive a health-based fund, given that one-third of M āori are poor and
destitute, where a sole parent looks afte r many children? What positive schemes are
there for these children in mainstream schools?]

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: He maha ng ā ūmanga kua whakat ūria e m ātau i roto i
te taha mō te mātauranga kei roto i ngā kura, i roto i ng ā whānau e noho pōhara kei roto
i ngā kāinga. Nāku i whakat ū e 70 ng ā kaimahi e mahi ana kei roto i ng ā whānau, ngā
hāpori. M ā rātau e mahi ana, i te 600 wh ānau ki te tautoko i a r ātau i roto i t ō rātau
pōharatanga, me ā mātau mahi M āra Kai. Kua tukuna atu ki te iwi, e 300 m āra kai kua
tukuna atu ki te iwi, me ērā atu āhuatanga. E pai ana te pātai, koinā tā mātau.
[We have established several enterprises in  terms of educati on in schools and in
families living in poverty. I have establishe d 70 positions for people to work within
families and communities. They worked al ongside 600 families to support them through
their state of impoverishment. We have our M āra Kai initiative—we granted 300
vegetable gardens to tribes—and other sche mes. It is a good question, and that is our
position on it.]

items.speaker: Hon Nanaia Mahuta
items.text: He take wero tēnei, Mr Speaker. Ko te tino ngako o taku pātai
e p ā ana ki ng ā kaupapa kei roto i ng ā kura auraki, m ō ēnei tamariki p ōhara, ēnei
tamariki rawakore.
[I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The gi st of my question related to initiatives in
mainstream schools for children living in poverty.]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member’s question was somewhat longer than that, and
being a supplementary question, th e Minister is not required to answer just the last part
of the question. Even though the question may have been in Te Reo, the same rules
apply to the answering of the question. The question covered more than just that issue.

items.speaker: Hon Nanaia Mahuta
items.text: Ka p ātai atu ki te Whare kia whakaw ātea te w āhanga māku
kia tuku te pātai anō.
[I seek leave of the House for me to ask my question once more.]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought for the member to ask her question again. Is there
any objection to that course of action? There is no objection.

items.speaker: Hon Nanaia Mahuta
items.text: T ēnā koutou. He aha te whakatau o te Minita m ō ēnei
tamariki p ōhara, ēnei tamariki rawakore? He aha ng ā tino kaupapa i roto i ng ā kura
auraki hei awhiawhi i ēnei tamariki e kōrerotia ake nei?
[Thank you collectively. What consideration has he made for these impoverished and
destitute children? What are the main pr ogrammes in mainstream schools to assist
these children referred to here?]

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: N ā mātau i whakat ūria ētahi h ōtaka m ō te p ānui
pukapuka mō ngā mea iti kei roto i ngā kura decile 1, 2, and 3 katoa o te motu. Nā mō te
pōharatanga, mō te kai, kua tukuna atu t ētahi pūtea ki ēnei wh ānau kia whakat ū māra
kai. Atu ki tēnā arā ngā kaimahi e mahi ana i roto, i waenganui a rātau.
[We established reading programmes for th e little ones in a ll decile 1, 2, and 3
schools throughout the country. In terms of po verty and food, we pr ovided funding to
these families to plant gardens. Aside from that, we have workers working amongst and
with them.]
4014 Questions for Oral Answer 26 Jul 2012

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does the Minister agree with the human rights commissioner that
keeping a third of M āori children in poverty infringes th eir fundamental right to well-
being, and that one fair way to alleviate that poverty would be to lift the minimum wage
to a livable level?

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: He maha ngā huarahi kia taea e tātau ki te whakamāmā
i te w āhanga kei roto i a r ātau e noho p ōhara ana. Ehara m ā te K āwanatanga anake,
engari m ō tātau katoa, ng ā hap ū, ng ā rohe, ng ā komiti, ng ā wh ānau katoa mai i ng ā
mema Pāremata. Kei a tātau katoa te rongoā kia whakamāmā ai te taha ki te taha pōhara.
Kaua e waiho mā te Kāwanatanga anake.
[There are several avenues that allow us to make the lives of those in poverty easier.
It is not just up to the Government but to all of us: subtribes, regions, committees,
families, and even members of Parliament. We have the remedy to ease impoverishment.
Do not leave it for the Government alone.]

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does the Minister, then, agree that the human right of M āori children
to adequate health care is infringed by the Government’s increase in prescription
charges when we know that 14 percent of M āori do not pick up prescriptions now
because of the cost?

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: He wā uaua mō tātau i tēnei wā. He ōhanga whakaheke
i tēnei wā. Nā reira, ko ētahi mea e taumaha ana, whakataumahatia o t ātau iwi. Ko ētahi
atu e whakapiki ai tā rātau noho. Nā reira, kāre he rongoa atu, nāku te kōrero i tēnā mea
anake ēngari, mō ng ā mea katoa. Mehemea ka taea e t ātau ki te whakam āmā ai, ki te
whakangāwari ai te noho o rātau e pōhara ana, ka pai ki ahau.
[This is a difficult time for everyone as we are in an economic recession. Therefore,
there are some things that make it heavy going for our people, or a burden upon them.
So there are no solutions, but this is my persona l view not only for this situation but for
everything. If we can make the lives of those living in poverty that much easier and
smoother, then that would do me nicely.]

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does the Minister, then, also agree that the human right of M āori
children to decent housing is breached by the Government’s cuts to State and social
housing provisions, which currently condemn 28 percent of M āori children to living in
overcrowded homes?

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: Ko taku k ōrero ehara m ō te K āwanatanga ēngari, mō
mātau. Kaha m ātau ki te tautoko i te K āwanatanga kia whakamahanatia ētahi o ng ā
whare e makariri ana. E 20,000 whare kua āwhinatia e mātau e te P āti Māori, kia noho
mahana ai a rātau tamariki.
[My statement is not on behalf of  the Government but for us, the M āori Party. We
have supported the Government strongly in the strategy to warm up cold homes. We, the
Māori Party, have assisted 20,000 homes to ensure that their children are warm.]

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I just want to clarify with you. It
could be an issue to do with translation, but  during question time it has been very clear
that Ministers are answering on behalf of  the Government, not on behalf of their
individual political parties, and twice in question time, in the interpretation—I do not
speak Te Reo M āori, so I just want to check that I am correct here—the Minister has
indicated he is replying on behalf of the Māori Party, not on behalf of the Government.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member is quite correct that Ministers are replying in their role
as a Minister, as part of the Government. Ho wever, they are at liberty to introduce into
their answers other material if it helps them answer the question asked. The risk they
face in doing that is if they bring into thei r answer material to do with their party, they
can then be asked about that, when norma lly they cannot be asked about that. The
Minister is not normally answerable in this House for matters to do with the M āori
Party. However, the Minister has, as the member points out, on a couple of occasions
26 Jul 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 4015
introduced the M āori Party into his answer s, and, therefore, the Minister can be asked
about those matters that he has covered in his answers.

items.speaker: Te Ururoa Flavell
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Kia ora t ātau. He aha t ā Whānau Ora, ki
te whakapiki i te ora o ngā tamariki Māori?
[Thank you, Mr Speaker. Greetings, everyone. What does Whānau Ora do to improve
the health of Māori children?]

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: Ki tāku mōhio, kei roto i te Whānau Ora he huarahi kia
whakapiki ai te ora o te wh ānau, ka tahi, o te tamaiti, ka rua. M ā te mahi ng ātahi o ngā
tari Kāwanatanga me te tautoko i te wh ānau kia noho p ūmau, kātahi ka whai w āhi ērā
momo wh ānau kia eke ki ng ā pūkenga, kia eke ki ō rātau wawata, me ō rātau hiahia
katoa. Nā reira, hoki aku kōrero ki ērā kōrero e pā ana ki te mahi i tēnei momo mahi mō
tātau katoa ehara m ā te K āwanatanga anake, ehara m ā Whānau Ora anake. Ka hoki au
ki tērā whakatauākī Māori “Mā tāu rourou, me tāku rourou ka ora ai te iwi”.
[I understand that Wh ānau Ora is a pathway to improve, one, family health, and,
two, the child. Government departments work ing together and s upporting the stability
of families will provide opportunities for those kinds of families to upskill and realise all
their desires and aspirations. And so I go back to my assertions to those statements
relating to this kind of work  being done by all of us and not by the Government or
Whānau Ora alone. I go back to that M āori proverb “Through your food basket and
mine we will ensure that the people survive”.]

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Given that 93,000 M āori children have parents on a benefit, does he
accept that the welfare reforms trap the child ren of beneficiaries into severe poverty,
and are therefore an active discrimina tion against the human rights of the M āori
children of those families?

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: Ahakoa kei a au ētahi whakaaro e p ā ana ki t ēnā pātai,
ko tēnā pātai te pātai mō te Minita mō tērā āhuatanga.
[Although I have my own views about that ques tion, it should really  be directed at
the Minister responsible for that situation.]

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. This question was set down for
the Minister of Māori Affairs. The question directly relates to the impact of Government
policy on M āori children. It is within his mini sterial responsibilit y to answer the
question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think the member makes a fair point that the Minister of M āori
Affairs has a broad area of responsibility. The primary question asked about the basic
human rights of children alleged to be in poverty, and the supplementary question that
was asked did cover those issues. I invite Metiria Turei to repeat her question.

items.text: Given that 93,000 M āori children have parents on a benefit, does he
accept that the welfare reforms trap the child ren of beneficiaries into severe poverty,
and are therefore an active discrimi nation against the human rights of M āori children in
those families?

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: Kāre anō kia oti te arotake o ēnā kōrero, tēnā pepa. Kei
te whiriwhiri tonu te K āwanatanga i ēnā kaupapa ēngari ko taku k ōrero, ko ētahi o ng ā
mea hōu ka pēhi ki runga i tētahi rōpū kei roto i te iwi wh ānui, ko ētahi atu e whakapiki
ai te ora kei roto i a rātau.
[The review of those comments and the paper are yet to be completed. The
Government is still negotiating those policies, but from me, some of the new initiatives

the well-being within them.]

items.text: Given that under the National-led Government the interests of

items.text: Will the Minister commit to seeking Cabinet approval to replace the

items.speaker: Metiria Turei

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think the member is making a fair point in that the Minister in his

Minister would recommend to the Government  that it should remove the distinction
between the children of parents who are working and those whose parents are not
working in respect of the Working for Fam ilies tax credit. I do not think it is a
satisfactory answer to that to say that the M āori Party has given its views to the

Tariana Turia to repeat her question—I beg your pardon, Metiria Turei! My apologies.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I do not mind being mistaken for Tariana, not at all. Will the Minister

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: I roto i ā mātau kōrero i te tēpu āe.

Companies and Limited Partnerships—Changes to Governance and Registration
and Actions of Associate Minister
5. KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI (National)  to the Minister of Commerce :
What steps is the Government taking to he lp maintain New Zealand’s reputation as a
trusted place to do business?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: This week the Companies and
Limited Partnerships Amendment Bill had its fi rst reading. The bill seeks to strengthen
aspects of the rules applyi ng to the governance, registra tion, and reorganisation of
companies and limited partnerships. The reforms will help maintain New Zealand’s
reputation as a trusted place to do business and will prom ote investor confidence and
participation in New Zealand’s capital markets. The bill seeks to strike the right balance
between deterring the actions that threaten  the integrity of a company registration
system and maintaining the ease of busin ess for New Zealand companies. I look
forward to the select committee’s thoughts on the bill.

items.speaker: Kanwaljit Singh Bakshi
items.text: What other issues does the bill seek to address?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: The bill will require each comp any registered in New Zealand
to have a resident ag ent if there is no director living in New Zealand or an approved
26 Jul 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 4017
jurisdiction. It will give new powers to the Registrar of Companies to investigate and
deal with non-compliance with the Companie s Act. This includes the power to flag
companies on the register that are under in vestigation. These are but some of the
changes in the bill. I welcome the support of  all parties across the House in progressing
at least the first reading of this bill, a nd I welcome the select committee’s views on all
of these matters.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Would another step to mainta in New Zealand’s reputation as
a trusted place to do business be to stand dow n a Minister who solic its and receives at

items.text: The bill has got nothing to do with ministerial responsibility.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The bill was the subject of

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I accept the member’s point of order.  It is certainly consistent with
the primary question. I guess the Minister’s answer, though, is indicating that he, as a
Minister, has no responsibility  for whether other Minister s are stood down or not. I
believe that is what he was saying, and that is a fair answer, I think. But I fully accept
the question as being in order.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Would it help New Zealand to be seen as a trusted place to do
business if Ministers had sufficient capacity to remember when they receive $80,000 in
plain envelopes and/or paper bags?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: I do not know whether he is re ferring to—I will not go—the
bill as drafted has absolutely nothing to do with whatever that member is talking about.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I say to the Minister that, sadly, the question has got nothing
to do with a bill. The question asked what steps the Government is taking to help
maintain New Zealand’s reputation as a trusted place to do business. The Minister may
have intended—[ Interruption] Order! The Minister may ha ve intended that answer to
that question to allow him to talk about a bill, but supplementary questions are not
constrained. They are constrained only in so far as this primary question states what it
states. The question asked is in order. It  is hypothetical, but it cannot be ignored,
because the question is in order, given that primary question.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Should I put it again?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is this a point of order?

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Oh no, no, I am just offering to put it again in case the
Minister—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! No, I think the Minister can recollect the question.

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: I recollect there was a hypot hetical question, and there are
many things that affect New Zealand’s reputa tion. One of the best things we can do to
affect New Zealand’s international reputa tion as a good place to do business is to
continue the prudent economic management th at this Government started about 4 years
ago and is continuing to do so.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: In light of his desire to main tain New Zealand’s reputation as a
trusted place to do business, is he satisfi ed that the Hon John Ba nks has the required
ethical standards to be his Associate Minister of Commerce?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: I do not appoint Associate Ministers.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: In light of his desire to main tain New Zealand’s reputation as a
trusted place to do business, is it his inte ntion to withdraw th e delegations of the
Associate Minister of Comm erce, John Banks, in light of the revelations that he

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: These reflections reflect pretty  badly on the questioner. I have

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. You know, and I know,

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! No, order! The member is  now questioning the answer. The

Welfare Reforms—Policies Affecting Families
6. JACINDA ARDERN (Labour)  to the Minister for Social Development : Does
she stand by her statement that “if we are going to make a difference for the families
who are struggling, we need to  be able to invest in in terventions that we know will
work”; if so, what are her methods for developing policies that she knows will work?
Hon CHESTER BORROWS (Associate Mi nister for Social Development)  on
behalf of the Minister for Social Development : The Minister stands by her full
statement that was made with regard to th e new Social Policy Eval uation and Research
Unit in the restructured Families Commission, where she said: “If we are going to make
a difference for the families who are struggli ng, we need to be able to invest in
interventions that we know will work and that have had full evaluations. This new unit
will build a body of evidence that will  allow policy makers, non-governmental
organisations, and anyone wan ting to invest in social services to make informed
decisions about which programmes are e ffective for New Zealand families.” The
establishment of this unit is a key part of this Government’s focus to ensure we are
investing in what works.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think the point is a fair point. The Minister is perfectly at liberty to
say that he does not have the information to  answer the question, but I think the point
the Hon David Parker makes is correct. Th e primary question is not focused on the
Families Commission; it does not mention it. But the Minister’s answer is still perfectly

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Can she provide to the House a ny advice or evaluation to show
that the policy she announced on Michael Laws’ show on drug-testing beneficiaries will
26 Jul 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 4019
work, when a Government department is ru moured to have provided evidence to the

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: I have not been briefed in respect of comments she
made in respect of drug testing.
Le’aufa’amulia Asenati Lole-Taylor : T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker. E rau rangatira m ā,

Major Events Development Fund—Promotion of New Zealand
7. JACQUI DEAN (N ational—Waitaki) to the Minister for Economic

items.speaker: Development
items.text: How is the Major Events Develo pment Fund contributing to building
New Zealand’s profile overseas?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Government
is using the Major Events Development Fund to partner with organisers to attract,
retain, grow, and deliver high-quality major events for New Zealand. The purpose of the
4020 Questions for Oral Answer 26 Jul 2012
Government funding is to ensure lasting be nefits for New Zealand from hosting events,
promotion of the country overseas, international media exposure, increased tourism, and
job creation. For example, last week I attended the media launch of the 2013 Winter
Games, which will receive $1 million in suppo rt from the Major Events Development
Fund. In return for this, Winter Games NZ will provide extensive international
television opportunities to prom ote this country as a premier winter destination across
our key tourism and trade markets. It is estimated that the 2013 event will deliver
around 33,000 visitor nights and reach a glob al television audience of around 800
million viewers.

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: How will the development of the Winter Games benefit New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Government investment is designed to provide a
platform for the event to step  up to another leve l in 2013. It is intended to become one
of the world’s top three snow sports events  and to deliver the quality expected of a
world-leading event. It will be one of the bi ggest winter sports events, in fact, outside
the Winter Olympics. It is expected to increase the number of participants, spectators,
and international tourists attending the event. The Winter Games is just one of the many
major events that the Government has backed.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Hang on—who backed it first? Who backed it first? You’re
just a follower, just a follower.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE

Triathlon ITU World Championship Series, an d the World Masters Games. Trevor is

Migrant Workers—Immigration New Zealand Labour Market Testing
8. DARIEN FENTON (Labour)  to the Minister of Immigration : What labour
market testing requirements does Immigrati on New Zealand carry out before approving
an employer’s application to bring foreign workers to New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: I have been advised by
Immigration New Zealand that it undertakes  a variety of labour-market checks, where
information from Work and Income, recruitment efforts by the employers, and the skills
shortage lists are taken into account. In the case of approva l in principle applications,
consultation is also undertak en with relevant unions, gu ilds, and industry training
organisations. The labour-market test is th ere to ensure that migrant workers do not
displace New Zealanders from employment opportunities.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: Is he confident th at labour-market testin g processes are robust
enough to protect New Zealand jobs, when Im migration New Zealand has just granted
approval in principle to one company to br ing in 110 so-called façade installers from
China on the basis that there are no suitable Ne w Zealanders able to either do the work
or be trained to do the work?

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: Yes, I am satisfied in the system.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: What specific actions, if any, do es Immigration New Zealand take
to ensure that the job prerequisites are not overstated or exa ggerated in order to
artificially exclude New Zealand residents from consideration for work?

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: As I mentioned in the answer to the primary question, there is
a very robust process that is  worked through with Work a nd Income, with the industry
training organisation providers, with the guild s, and with the unions. There is a very
robust process in place, and I am satisfied with that process.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: In what part of the Government’s 120-point economic plan does it
state that we will grow our economy and create jobs by bringing in migrant workers into
26 Jul 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 4021
temporary and fixed-term employment, despite New Zealanders being ready and able to
do this work or easily trained to do it?

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: I am pleased that that memb er is applauding our 120-point
plan, which is very successf ul. It is interesting that Labour brought in the Recognised
Seasonal Employer scheme, and if I could ju st quote from one of its members at the
time, a quote that is all about migrant workers in—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am not sure that is exactly an answer to the question asked.
It was not that specific a question, but the answer should relate to the question and not
wander a long way from it. If the Minister is not sure of the questi on, I invite Darien
Fenton to repeat it.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: In what part of the Government’s 120-point economic plan does it
state that we will grow our economy and create jobs by bringing in migrant workers into
temporary and fixed-term employment, despite New Zealanders being ready and able to
do this work or easily trained to do it?

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: As the member knows, we do require in our New Zealand
economy some foreigners, to ensure that we  can continue to grow our economy. If I

“There are always anxieties about the Recognised Seasonal Employer scheme—about

in this case that it is actually creating jobs  for New Zealand workers.” I agree with Mr

items.text: I seek leave to tabl e a letter from the Amalgamated Workers Union
to Minister Kate Wilkinson, asking for a revi ew of the decision to allow 110 workers to
be employed on façade construction, on the basi s that the skill requ ired is basic and
New Zealanders could be trained to do this work—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Leave is sought to tabl e that document. Is there any

Emissions Trading Scheme—Proposed Amendments
9. Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM (Green) to the Minister for Climate Change Issues:
Is the $328 million additional cost of the Government’s recent Emissions Trading
Scheme proposed amendments consistent w ith the National Party election pledge that
the amendments would be fiscally neutral?
Hon SIMON BRIDGES (Associate Mini ster for Climate Change Issues) on
behalf of the Minister for Climate Change Issues : Yes, because we do not want the
emissions trading scheme to be a tax-gra bbing revenue earner from households and the
productive sector. We also wa nted to amend our scheme, in  globally fragile conditions,
in the interests of the wider economy, ra ther than on the basis of some narrow
Government interest.

items.speaker: Dr Kennedy Graham
items.text: Why is the Government increas ing subsidies to emitters, in
these globally fragile conditions, to the tune  of several hundred million dollars, rather
than strengthening the emissions trading scheme so that it will actually reduce
emissions?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I do not agree with the basic premise of the question. They
are not subsidies; they are the absence of  a cost imposed on households and businesses
in this country.

items.speaker: Dr Kennedy Graham
items.text: Why does not the Government follow the UK model, which
has a binding 80 percent cut by 2050, with  5-yearly carbon budgets for reducing
emissions, instead of simply stating a weaker target with no credible plan to get there?
4022 Questions for Oral Answer 26 Jul 2012

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I have not examined the UK scheme in any great detail,
but it is fair to say we do not want the economic mess that they are in today.

items.speaker: Dr Kennedy Graham
items.text: Rather than weakening the emissions trading scheme, why
does the Government not introduce a plan, su ch as the British one—and I recommend
that the Associate Minister read it—that is  described as providing “a clear, credible,
long-term framework for a move to a low- carbon … economy, [giving] businesses and
individuals the … certainty they need to play their part.”?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I believe that in our emissions trading scheme we have
that clear, credible scheme, and we are als o, of course, wanting to make sure that in
these fragile economic conditions globally we do not ratchet it up unduly at this time.
Paid Parental Leave—Minister’s Statements
10. SUE MORONEY (Labour) to the Minister of Finance: Does he stand by all of
his statements on the proposed extension to paid parental leave?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes, particularly the statement that
the Government supports parents and fa milies. We have spent $154 million on
providing the current paid parental leave,  which has increased by $67 per week since
2008. Alongside that, the Government spends $1.4 billion on early childhood education
subsidies and $2.6 billion on Working for Families payments. We have made sure that
despite Budgets being tight a nd despite a recession, we have  at least maintained all
these payments to families.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Does he stand by his statement in April that the bill to extend paid
parental leave would require an extra $500 million in borrowing over the next 3 to 4
years?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Did he receive advice from the Department of Labour on 11 April,
the day he announced his intention to use a financial veto, that  showed that the
maximum cost of the bill was $285.6 million over 3 years—almost half the figure he
misled the public with?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: If you add the number for the 4 th year, they are pretty
similar.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: No, they’re not.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: They are. The simple point is the member’s proposition will
double the cost of paid parental  leave. I look forward to the day when the Government
has those sorts of choices. We do not have those choices now. We are working hard to
maintain the current expenditure of $154 m illion on paid parental leave, $1.4 billion on
early childhood subsidies, which have increas ed by 40 percent in the last 4 years, and
$2.6 billion on Working for Families payments. We are supporting families very
extensively.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: I seek leave to table a documen t from the Department of Labour,
released under the Official Information Act to me, which shows that the maximum cost
of the paid parental leave bill over 3 years would be $285.6 million.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection?
There is objection.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Did he tell journalists at a press conference he held that he will not
extend paid parental leave, even after the Government  books get back into surplus,
when he announced his intention to use a financial veto, on 11 April?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: It is not a matter of whether I will extend paid parental
leave. What I did announce was that in my stat utory role as Minister of Finance I would
be vetoing this particular bill because of th e high cost of it at this time. Of course
Governments have got choices in the future, and those choices will all be fairly difficult.
26 Jul 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 4023
Paid parental leave will be only one of a l ong list of aspirations New Zealanders will
have once the Government gets its books back into surplus.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Spea ker. The question was very direct. I
asked him whether he had told journalists a particular statement. He did not respond to
the question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: What I will do—because I cannot recollect exactly the question
asked—is I will allow the member to repeat her question, but it had better ask just that.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. It does ind eed. Did he tell journalists at a
press conference he held that he will not extend paid parental leave, even after the
Government books get back into surplus, wh en he announced his intention to use a
financial veto, on 11 April?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, I cannot recall exactly th e words that were used, but I
can tell the member that it is not a matte r of my extending paid  parental leave. I
announced that, as Minister of Finance, in  my statutory capacity—as used many times

Fishing Vessels—Changes to Design and Construction Rule
11. JAMI-LEE ROSS (National—Botany)  to the Associate Minister of

items.speaker: Transport
items.text: What recent changes has the Governme nt made to improve the safety of
fishing boats?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Today I announced
changes to the maritime rule covering the design and construction of fishing boats and
the equipment used on them. The rule applies to vessels less than 25 metres in length,
which make up more than 90 percent of the fi shing fleet. The fishi ng industry is one of
our most dangerous, and structural and equipment failures count for approximately one-
fifth of fishing industry injuries. The new requirements will mitigate the risks such as of
fire and flooding, and substantial new structural requirements will be applied to newly
constructed vessels.

items.speaker: Jami-Lee Ross
items.text: How do these changes reinforce the Government’s focus on better
and less regulation?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: These changes are part of a bigger story in transport,
where we are working with industry on reducing both unnecessary compliance costs
and red tape while improving safety as well . Other recent examples include regulations
regarding jetboat licences and passenger service vehicles. Industry involvement on these
changes has been essential to ensuring that rules are appropriate and workable for the
sector.

items.text: I appreciate the spirit in which th e point of order is raised, but we

radio transcripts, or anything like that that are readily av ailable to members. We have

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think the member makes a useful point of order, in that on an
important occasion like this it is unhelpful if we commence the debate while so many
members are moving around the House and while visitors are entering  the gallery. We

intending to leave the Chamber to please do so, so that once we start the debate the
House is not further disrupted by pe ople moving about. I will defer calling the
honourable Minister for just a moment longer. Just so th e public knows what is going
on, I have just deferred the commencement of  the third reading de bate on Government
order of the day No. 1 while members are leav ing the Chamber, to give the Minister a
more dignified environment in which to make an important speech on this very
important Treaty settlement legislation. I th ink the House is now in a rather quieter

Hon TARIANA TURIA (Minister for Whānau Ora) on behalf of the Minister for

items.speaker: Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations
items.text: I move, That the Rongowhakaata Claims Settlement
Bill be now read a third time. Mai i ngā kāhui maunga o Whanganui tae noa ki a koutou
o ng ā maunga Puketapu, Manawar ū hoki, ka t ū ahau ki te tuku mihi ki a koutou o
Rongowhakaata, ngā uri o Te Kooti Rikirangi hoki kua takahi te papa kia tae mai nei ki
te Whare P āremata m ō te p ānuitanga tuatoru ō tō koutou piri. Ki a koutou, ng ā
kaumātua, ngā kuia, ngā koroua, tēnā koutou katoa.
[From the cluster mountains of Whanganui, to you of the mountains Puketapu and
Manawarū as well, I rise to extend a welc ome to you of Rongowhakaata, and of the
descendants of Te Kooti Riki rangi, too, who have traversed the countryside to arrive
here at Parliament House for the third reading of your bill. To you all, the elders,
elderly women and menfolk, greetings.]
One hundred and twenty years ago in Apr il 1893, Te Kooti Rikirangi uttered these
unforgettable words: “Ko te waka he hoehoenga mō koutou i muri i ahau nā te ture tērā.
Mā te ture an ō te ture e aki. The canoe that you mu st paddle when I am gone is that of
the law. Only the law can be pitched against the law.” Today that prophecy comes to
fruition. The Rongowhakaata Claims Settlement Bill will finally settle the historical
Treaty of Waitangi claims of Rongowhakaata.
The settlement journey for Rongowhakaata and Ng ā Uri o Te Kooti Rikirangi has
been a long one. Many who have borne the weight  of this journey are no longer with us
today, and we acknowledge and remember them. The Waitangi Tribunal’s 2004 report
concluded that T ūranga’s history includes some of the darkest and most dramatic
moments in our nation’s history. The tri bunal described the breaches arising from
Crown military action against the iwi as some of the worst in New Zealand. But it went
further and laid a challenge th at I believe it is incumbent on all of us to pick up. The
tribunal noted that it could not help but think that the unsettled state of relations
between Māori and P ākehā is in part due to the fact that these stories are remembered
only by tangata whenua and a few specialist historians. This leaves the nation in an
unenviable state of flux, a nd I quote from the 2004 repo rt: “While only one side
remembers the suffering of the past, dialogue will always be difficult. One side
commences the dialogue with anger and the other side has no idea why. Reconciliation
cannot be achieved by this means.” How do we avoid repeating the mistakes of the
past? What price is paid for the oppressive policies and injustices suffered in the name
of the law?
This settlement records the Crown’s d eep remorse over wrongs done. The apology
expresses profound regret that  over the generations to th e present day Crown actions
26 Jul 2012 Rongowhakaata Claims Settlement Bill 4027
have significantly impacted on Rongowhakaat a’s social and trad itional structures,
autonomy, and ability to exercise customary rights and responsibilities. The apology is a
sincere attempt to report the Crown’s failure since 1840 to respect the mana of
Rongowhakaata and their rangatir atanga. It is difficult for a nyone outside of this iwi to
truly appreciate the depth of  loss and prejudice that has been suffered. The words of a
young 17-year-old give voice to that grief,  which has endured over generations. W ētini
Wilkins-Larkin, a direct descendant of Te K ooti Rikirangi, told the story of his nannies,
Hine Campbell and Mihi Larkin. “This str uggle”—he said—“goes back in history, to
the time even when my grandmother wa s a young school girl who experienced the
stigma and shame of being a direct des cendant of the koroua. I’m told that the
Matawhero massacre would be a common topic in the school curriculum, and that my
Nan would often be a scapegoat for other pupi ls, that the finger was pointed to her in
disgust and that she would even hide under the shadow of her desk, with her face hidden
behind her hands.” What a painful memory to live with throughout your life. How do
Ngā Uri o Te Kooti Rikirangi move past the stigmatisation of Te Kooti and his
descendants? It will take time, and our greates t hope is that in the course of the journey
we witness today, we will reach a time when all New Zealanders look on Te Kooti as
the founder of Te Haahi Ringat ū, acknowledge his inspirational leadership, and
appreciate his commitment to the preservation of Te Reo me ōna tikanga, just as his
followers from my own iwi continue to follow and believe today.
This bill expresses that recognition and redress for the bitter grievances of
Rongowhakaata that are long overdue. That recognition includes knowledge that the
Crown used force in T ūranga in November 1865 when there was absolutely no need to
do so. The Crown’s attack on Waerenga a Hika, whose occupants included women and
children, was unwarranted and unj ust and caused severe and l ong-term prejudice to this
iwi. The summary executions at Ng ātapa by Crown forces in 1869 tarnished the honour
of the Crown and will live on in the hear ts and minds of Rongowhakaata descendants,
their w’ ānau, and their hap ū. The indefinite detention in harsh conditions on the
Chatham Islands without trial or the laying of charges was an injustice depriving
Rongowhakaata of their basic human rights. The enduring cruelty of Crown actions was
epitomised in the 1869 deed of cession, resultin g in the extinguishment of all of their
customary land interests. In effect, the Crown confiscated Rongowhakaata land,
including interests in over 50,000 acres at Patutahi, and by exclusion from titles
awarded by the Poverty Bay Commission.
On days like this it is unimaginable,  the sadness deep w ithin the soul of
Rongowhakaata, nor can the ongoing feelings about the Crown actions be put into
words.
The illegal imprisonment of a quarter of the adult male population of T ūranga on
Wharekauri, and the loss in the war of an estimated 43 percent of  their adult male
population, including the illegal execution of a third to a half of that number, were
described by the tribunal as a “stain on our  national history and character”. The final
chapter in the tribunal’s report, “Hei Whak amahutanga: The Healing” Is headed with
these words: “Whakamoea nga patu ki nga patu rakau, kia whanau ko te pai. Put to
sleep the evil words and weapons of war so that goodness can prevail.”
One of the ways in which resolution may be achieved is in addressing the
confiscation of Te Hau ki T ūranga, the elaborate w’are whakairo carved by the expert
carver Raharuhi Rukupō of Ngāti Kaipoho. Crown troops took possession of Te Hau in
1867 in the aftermath of Waerenga a Hika. The acquisition of this cherished tribal
whare, which is held by Te Papa here in Wellington, has been a source of great pain to
this iwi, and it is right that redress relating to  Te Hau lies at the heart of this settlement.
The settlement legislation contains within it the vesting in Rongow hakaata of sites of
4028 Rongowhakaata Claims Se ttlement Bill 26 Jul 2012
significance, funding for cultural rev italisation, specific redress for Ng ā Uri o Te Kooti
Rikirangi, a range of commercial redress properties, and other elements of redress. This
will assist Rongowhakaata in rebuilding thei r economic platform for the benefit of
present and future generations.
We bear an enduring debt of gratitude to  this iwi, who have demonstrated great
generosity to the nation in  foregoing full compensation. To day there will be time for
recognition to acknowledge th e significant journey, which started in 1992 when H ēni
Sunderland, Peter Gordon, Darcy Ria, and Stan  Pardoe lodged their claims. There will
no doubt be tears shed and memories shared as Rongowhakaata trace over the steps that
led to this day. And in the midst of the hear tache I hope there is also room to remember
the statement of Wetini Wilkins-Larkin, who ended his submission as the voice of hope:
“We have regained and restored the mana that we so deserved, and can now hold our
heads high when saying ‘I am a direct de scendant of Te Kooti Rikirangi.’ ” N ā reira,
tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, tēnā tātou katoa.

items.speaker: Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA
items.text: I a koutou o te hau
kāinga e whai kaha atu i konei, i te w āhi o te Whare M īere, e mihi kau ana ki a koutou
ngā tūpakeke. E tautoko atu ng ā whakaaro i puta ā-waha a Tariana me r ātou mā ki ng ā
koroua, ngā kuia p ērā i a H ēni, te wahine kaha ki te mahi toi, p ēnā i a Darcy m ō tana
mahi i roto i te Tari M āori, me t ērā a Pita e mahi ana i t ōna mahi i konei i ng ā tari, i a
rātou, me koe, e Stan, ko koe kē te mea e ora ana. E mihi kau ana ki a koe. Tēnā koe mō
tēnā e Rēhia, koutou katoa, e Willie, ng ā mea pakeke, e mihi kau ana, t ēnā koutou. E te
pāpā Noel, ahakoa k āre au i t īmata atu ki te mihi i ng ā manuhiri, e mihi kau ana ki a
koutou. E tuku mihi ki w ēnei, ki te whanaunga a Willie, a matua Stan, a Meka, a Jodie
Wyllie mō tō rātou whakatoi kia oti atu te mahi nei. Me koutou katoa e mahi atu ng ā
mahi e rere atu te taea whakahuri ki te rangi oti nei.
He tino rangi pai atu t ēnei. E kite atu t ātou o te Whare M īere e manaaki atu kia oti
pai. Nō reira. tēnā koutou. Mō rātou e rere atu. ngā hunga pērā i a Addie, a Huia, e tangi
hoki te ng ākau. Ēngari mō koutou e ora ana, ko t ēnei anō tō kaha o Rongowhakaata e
tae atu i konei. Mōhio atu tātou mō ngā kōrero o te mahi o nga hōia. I rongo koutou ngā
tupuna, ngā pakopako o ng ā pū pērā atu te mahinga atu. N ō reira, e tautokotia atu ng ā
kōrero o te tuahine me tātou katoa i konei.
[To those from home who made a great effort to get here to the place of the Beehive,
to you, the elders, I welcome you. I endorse  the sentiments exp ressed by Tariana and
others to the elderly men and womenfolk like H ēni, that great artist; Darcy, his work in
the Māori department, and Pita, for his work among departments here. You too, Stan,
the one still alive, I congratulate you. I acknowledge you for your contribution, R ēhia,
all of you, Willie, the ex perienced ones, I applaud you a ll, well done. I acknowledge
you, Noel, the father figure. Even though I did not begin the tributes  to the visitors, I
extend a welcome to you collectively. I welcom e these ones, as well: Willie, the relative,
uncle Stan, Meka, Jodie Wyllie, for being che eky so that this ma tter would be done and
dusted—in fact, all of you who set about to complete your task s to turn things round to
get to this day.
This is indeed a wonderful day. We of the B eehive will make sure that it is completed
well. So I commend you. As for those who have passed aw ay, like Addie and Huia, I
mourn for them, too. As for you, the living, your efforts to get here, Rongowhakaata, is
greatly admired. We know what the militia di d, we know the stories. You, the elders,
heard the musket fire and the havoc it created. So I endorse the sentiments expressed by
the sister colleague and all of us here.]
I want to mention Maever and Peter Moeau and the part of this claim relating to Ng ā
Uri o Te Kooti Rikirangi. Certainly, Te Kooti’s deeds and the reasoning behind them
are things that are etched in  history. That he was a trader of some knowledge and was
26 Jul 2012 Rongowhakaata Claims Settlement Bill 4029
into commerce is something that is very interesting. That he was put asunder, for
whatever reason, it is indeed great that we ar e here today to put all that to rest. He
travelled away. He was imprisoned. Certainly, the Ringatū Hāhi still survives today, and
I want to mihi to them and to the uri.
Before I start I want to say that it is a great day, and, be fore I forget, mihi to the
Ministers—Minister Turia a nd co., and especially Mr Fi nlayson. I always thought Mr
Cullen was the better of the Ministers, but I think Mr Fi nlayson might end up being not
too bad, actually. I want to recognise his ab ility, because he knows I am going to set to
on him about some of these things in here . But I do want to mention him, and the
officials, as at times they are sorely forgotten. I do want to mention and mihi to him.
So, Te Kooti Rikirangi, those things and the preserved art forms in several of the
houses around the country stand as a signal and a sign to his following and his uri who
are still surviving. The fascinating thing is , in my mind, being a scholar of Treaty
settlements and understanding most of them, I would say that ther e is not one worse
than this Treaty settlement in terms of what the Crown did to our people in this country.
And I am not saying that because they are sitting in the gallery; it is a fact. It was one of
the most dastardly actions ever perpetrated, ever set to upon any iwi, tribe, or whānau in
this country. Today, that we bring it to rest is something that we should be proud of as
politicians.
Raharuhi Rukup ō was a master carver, and he certa inly left his etched signal. I
thought I would start off here, Minister, with Te Hau ki T ūranga, just in case I forgot
and the bell rang. Thank you for its return. Thank you for making sure that it goes back.
I was fascinated to read in the summar y here about what would happen, and the
resources and the support that  would go to, particularly, its  relocation. I th ink that is
great—that it is to be resourced. But I recall when the M āori land incorporations were
returned, a lot of the people jumped at it and accepted it. That house has been down here
for a long time, so we should consider ensu ring that the ongoing costs of running and
maintaining it are put in here. I read it ve ry carefully. There is a lot of talk about
resourcing the relocation of it but not about  the continuation of both preserving it and
making sure that these people are able to be paid to look after it, to be frank, because
they have shared it with the nation for a long, long time. There are ongoing costs.
You know, this is amazing. These people, th e Crown set to on them. Te Kooti did
some interesting things amongst them, and for a people to forgive that takes a lot of
gumption. For people to accept that that happ ened and try to get to a better place
amongst themselves, not just with the Cr own, is something that they should be
respected for, because that is exactly what they have done. The thing about history—sad
history and bad history—is if you look back too much all you get is a sore neck. At the
moment, it is a great day for them to be here.
Prior to 1865 Rongowhakaata had full control of all their resources. They were in
control of them, they were running businesse s, and they were looking after themselves
and the early settlers. When war broke  out, Rongowhakaata a dopted a policy of
neutrality, which is fascin ating because some of these people have been branded
rebels—I am not sure which ones of them, but they were branded rebels. They took a
neutral stance. It is fascinating that the Crown did not respect that peace, that it set to on
them, not lightly, harder than over in Tarana ki—it blasted them. It certainly shows that
the Crown enacted military force to take a position—both lands and resources—and to
disenfranchise them, not just from what th ey had of their own but also to set up the
empire’s flag to flutter over the top of them  and suggest that they are not needed. Well,
they have stood the test of time. They are he re today. They have a whakapapa and, as I
debated last week, when somebody said th at the Crown is returning their mana,
Rongowhakaata never lost their mana, like any of these iwi—never, ever, ever. The two
4030 Rongowhakaata Claims Se ttlement Bill 26 Jul 2012
scholars over there who were waxing lyrical ab out that last week need to think again.
They never lost their mana. That it was impinged on and it was wounded here and there
does not mean to say they lost it. Their tino rangatiratanga has certainly stood the test of
time.
As Minister Turia said, the Crown’s attack on Waerenga a Hika, which included a lot
of women and children, was abhorrent, to sa y the least. It was one of the worst war
situations in this country. And the ongoing lo oting by the military forces after that is
something that we need to remember and get rid of. It is a bit like a movie,
Rongowhakaata’s history, because some of them  got sent to the Chathams with no trial
conducted in the courts. They were sent th ere and locked up. It shows their tenacity,
because they escaped after 2 years. If you have  ever been to the Chatham Islands like I
have, on an aeroplane, I do not know how the hang they escaped. But they must have
been pretty smart people to escape, and they escaped. Then other things happened. The
summary executions at Ngātapa by the Crown forces in January 1869 were the worst, in
my mind. That people were lined up against th e cliffs. That they were torn apart by
some overzealous young punk who had come from the empire is something that we
need to remember.
So they have been a very brave people, and it is a great day for them to be here to see
the end of it, and that Stan Pardoe is still living, for they chew his back every now and
again like we do most people in those positions. Stan is still here out of the four original
applicants. A lot of these people did this for nothing. That is why the Minister is serious
about the whare.
There is another matter, Minister, and I just want to read from the Crown’s
acknowledgment in subclause (17)(b) in clause 7: “t he pollution of T ūranga waterways
by Gisborne’s sewerage system and indus trial waste has had a severe effect on
Rongowhakaata, including the loss of many traditional sources of kai moana;” and blah-
blah-blah. On top of that it has got about th e forestry and the erosion and that. Well,
Minister, the sewage is still there. It is getting worse, actually. I suggested in the second
reading that it is not too late to stump up, and that is somethi ng that should be put right.
I would encourage you to know it a bit harder, Minister, because it is a continued
raupatu—that raw sewage pouring out. There is a local authority there. I hope Meng
Foon is watching this. We have go t a Chinese mayor who can speak M āori. Kite atu te
paru e tuku ana i te takutai moana [ You will see raw sewage released on to the
foreshore], dare I mention it.  I reira k ē te pirau o te tangata  e haere tonu atu. [ You will
see human waste floating away there.]
As I round up, can I encourag e you, Minister, to consider  that, on the way through.
Kia ora tātou.
Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON (Minister for Treaty of Waitangi
Negotiations): E ng ā mana, e ng ā reo, koutou m ā o Ng āti Rongowhakaata, nau mai,
haere mai, ki te Pāremata.
[To the authorities and languages, you of Ng āti Rongowhakaata, welcome, welcome
to Parliament.]
I am genuinely delighted, and that is no hype rbole, to speak in this third reading
debate. I became the Minister for Treaty of  Waitangi Negotiations in late November
2008, and I agreed with my officials that I would destroy their holiday and take them on
a hīkoi in mid-January 2009 so that I could meet some of the iwi that I would be dealing
with. So the first flight was up to Tair āwhiti and the first meeting was with the good
people who are in the gallery today. That is where I firs t met Stanley Pardoe, Kristen
Maynard, and others. So it has been, even since 2009, a long and somewhat convoluted
journey, but we are here t oday and I do acknowledge the ne gotiators, particularly you,
Stan. It has been great to get to know you a nd to work with you. I am just so pleased
26 Jul 2012 Rongowhakaata Claims Settlement Bill 4031
that we have reached this stage. I also wish to acknowledge others who have come from
Tūranganui a Kiwa to join us today, because this is a very, very important day in the life
of the country and this bill has its unique f eatures. It is not a mere deal, as some
insultingly describe it. It is a very important settlement of grievances that go to the heart
of our nation. It gives effect to a deed that Rongowhakaata have negotiated with the
Crown. It contains Crown acknowledgments that are very important—and I suggest that
if people do not know much about the history of what happened, they should read those
acknowledgments and they should read th e preamble—and the Rongowhakaata Claims
Settlement Bill also contains provisions for cultural and commercial redress.
It is very important to acknowledge the c ontribution of negotiators. It is not pro
forma thanks, because these negotiators in this particular matter have worked on this
claim for more than a decade. The tribunal held hearings in the early 2000s, and in 2004
the tribunal reported that the history of what went on in Tūranganui a Kiwa was marked
by grievous Crown breaches of the history a nd by some of the darkest moments in our
nation’s history. More than 40 percent of the men in T ūranganui a Kiwa died as a result
of Crown military action between 1865 and 1872.
Settlement negotiations with  the Crown began in 2005, and when Dr Cullen—well,
Sir Michael, as he is now—was the Mini ster in charge of Treaty of Waitangi
Negotiations an agreement in principle was signed, in September 2008. I was very
fortunate to be the Minister to work with the iwi to complete the detail of the settlement,
and we initialled the deed of settlement at what I thought was a very moving ceremony
at Te Papa in July last year. I have to sa y there was some considerable publicity both on
television and in the papers about the in itialling, and I was expecting quite some
negative emails to start flowing in—as so often they do—but I never received anything,
because I think people deep down acknowledged  that this was a taonga that did not
belong to Te Papa; it belonged to the pe ople of Rongowhakaata. Then the deed was
signed last spring, on a beautiful Friday morning in September.
I believe that it is very important for people to understand just what went on. Mrs
Turia has outlined the broad history, and I do not  think it is necessary or appropriate for
me to go over ground that has been so ably covered by her and also by Mr Horomia. But
I just want to focus on what for me is very much one of the highlights of this bill, and
that is the way in which we have managed to reach a resolution for Te Hau ki T ūranga,
because the Crown simply did come in and confiscate it in 1867. It was removed by
force, and it has been kept in various na tional museums ever si nce. Many alterations
have been made to Te Hau ki Tūranga without the consent of Rongowhakaata.
I always enjoyed the initial debates I ha d with some officials about the legal
ownership of Te Hau ki T ūranga. They were saying: “Well, you know, the statute said
that when Te Papa was created, all propert y of the old Dominion Museum transferred
over to Te Papa.” and it sounded all so very legal, but the reality of the matter is—as we
all know—that the ownership of Te Hau ki T ūranga was never surrendered by
Rongowhakaata; never handed over with their consent. That is  why it is very important
to note that clause 23 of the bill makes it clear beyond any doubt at all that Te Hau ki
Tūranga vests in the trustees nominated by Rongowhakaata.
I thought that the M āori Affairs Committee did a ve ry good job and its commentary
is worth referring to, because it said it is currently housed—

items.speaker: Hon Parekura Horomia
items.text: Good chairman.

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: Oh, it is not just the chair. We know that he
is a superstar, but there are others, as well, and being the generous soul he is, he would
be the first to acknowledge that.
The select committee heard that Rongowhakaat a do not wish the return of Te Hau ki
Tūranga to create a financial burden for future  generations, and it records that Te Papa
4032 Rongowhakaata Claims Se ttlement Bill 26 Jul 2012
and the Ministry for Culture and Heritage have committed themselves to working with
Rongowhakaata to ensure a sustainable future for the whare, particularly as regards its
relocation. I endorse 100 percent what Mr Horo mia said. It has been shared with the
nation for over 100 years; it is entirely fa ir and appropriate th at central government
makes a significant contribution to the ongoing costs. It is certainly not going to be a
situation where the Crown simply says to Rongowhakaata: “Well done. It is back in
your hands. You look after it.” So I am very  much looking forward to engaging with
Rongowhakaata—we have already started, but I am looking forward to the ongoing
engagement—to make sure that in the very n ear future we determine a way in which it
can be relocated to Tairāwhiti and that the financial redress of the settlement, which will
enable the iwi to build a fu ture for themselves in Tair āwhiti, will not be spent
disproportionately on Te Hau ki Tūranga.
Mrs Turia has also outlined the commercial and the financial redress, and I am not
going to repeat that. I just want to say to  the people of Rongowha kaata as, if you like,
the Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage that I am determined and I am very keen to
engage with them sooner rather than later so that we can work out when exactly Te Hau
ki Tūranga can go home and how the Crown can help.
There are many people who have contribute d to this settleme nt. I acknowledge Mr
Horomia, who was with me the day the deed was signed. I acknowledge Sir Michael
Cullen, who oversaw the prelimin ary negotiation of the agreement in principle. I guess
we all thought, did we not, in 2009 that it woul d be able to be signed up very quickly,
but there have been issues. They have required patience and determination—and I see

items.speaker: Stan Pardoe nodding. Probably he thinks
items.text: “Well,  Minister, that’s an  understatement.” I
acknowledge my ministerial co lleagues. I particularly acknowledge the Minister of
Māori Affairs, with whom I have so enjoye d working on this matte r; the Minister of
Conservation, who is always very gene rous when I come knocking about cultural
redress; and also the Minister for Land Information.
Many Government departments and offici als have also made very valuable
contributions. But, as I said in the Ng āti M ākino debate a couple of hours ago, one
expects that of officials and Ministers because that is our job, but there are people in the
gallery who have given, and given, and gi ven, over many years. They have given of
their own time, given of their weekends, and at some financial cost in order to reach this
stage. Very few people outside the negotiators  for the Crown and the officials, I think,
appreciate the sacrifices that the negotiato rs of Treaty settlements make on behalf of
their people, and I salute them for their tenacity, their good faith, and their courage.
In conclusion, all I want to say is that we have unfinished business—that is, the
Crown and Rongowhakaata. We have, hopefully, a strong ongoing relationship that will
blossom in the years to come, and I can think of no better first task for us to get on with
in that new relationship than to focus on Te Hau ki T ūranga to see what we can do,
because from my personal point of view, the sooner we can resolve that, the sooner that
Te Hau ki Tūranga goes home, the better.

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: Tēnā koe te Kaiwhakahaere o te
Whare. Tēnā kōrua e ngā minita, koutou r ā ngā mema o t ēnei Pāremata, tēnā koutou. E
aku rangatira, e ng ā iwi o T ūranga-nui-a-Kiwa, Rongowhakaata, Ngai T āmanuhiri, Te
Aitanga-a-Māhaki, t ēnā koutou. Nau mai, hara mai, whakatau mai ki te P āremata nei,
tēnā koutou, t ēnā koutou. Ā, mihi atu ki aku whanaunga n ō Te Wai Pounamu, n ō Kai
Tahu whānui kua tae mai nei ki te kaupapa o t ēnei rā, tēnā koutou. Huri noa i te Whare,
tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, kia ora tātou katoa.
[Greetings to you, Mr Speaker of the House, you two ministers, and indeed all you
members of this Parliament, salutations. I acknowledge you, my leaders, and people of
Gisborne, Rongowhakaata, Ngai T āmanuhiri, and Te Aitanga-a-M āhaki, greetings.
26 Jul 2012 Rongowhakaata Claims Settlement Bill 4033
Welcome, welcome, and welcome to this Parl iament, salutations. To my relatives from
the South Island and Kai Tahu at large, who ca me here for the matter of the day, I
commend you. Greetings, then, to you throughout the House, and to us all.]
Much has been said by the Minister fo r Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations and my
senior colleagues today in reference to the Rongowhakaata Claims Settlement Bill
before us. It gives me great pl easure to be here to speak at this, the final reading for
Rongowhakaata and ngā uri o Te Kooti Rikirangi. This bill is about them, and it is a real
honour.
A lot of comments have been made, and they are true, about the atrocities that were
committed against Rongowhakaata. They were heinous: Waerenga a Hika, Ng ātapa, the
detentions over at Wharekauri, and the conf iscations of their lands. I have spoken a lot
about those actions in my earlier speeches, so  I want to focus this final speech on some
other aspects of this bill and the settlement.
The return of the superb piece of artwork, the whare known as Te Hau ki T ūranga—
and I know the speakers before me have spoken a lot about the return  of that beautiful,
beautiful whare—and the ongoing preservation of that revered house will be of great
import to the descendants of th e master carver Raharuhi Rukup ō, and the wh ānau and
hapū of the Poverty Bay area. These people of  Rongowhakaata are an ingenious people,
quick to seize upon opportunities advantageous  to themselves, and were successful
international traders righ t up until 1865. Just the inge nuity of Rongowhakaata—the
