flight of the so-called rebels from Wharekauri to T ūranga is a classic example; my
matua here, Parekura, mentioned that. It is a classic example of what I speak of, and the
daring of those actions never ceases to amaze me. It was not much of a trick. They were
imprisoned for 2 years on a faraway land over there in Wharekauri, they overpowered
their guards, hatched a cunning plan to flag down a schooner,  and headed back home to
Tūranga-nui-a-Kiwa.
It seems to me that the only way to get to  and from the Chathams in those days was
to steal a boat, because Pōmare did it from Wellington in 1835—he did the round trip—
and Te Kooti and his crew did the return  trip back from the Chathams. Those M āoris
were not going to paddle their way back—i t is too far—but such was the ingenuity,
sheer willingness to survive, and drive to get back home that was demonstrated by the
illustrious tūpuna of Rongowhakaata, who are here to day. That is why I have absolute
faith in the uri of Rongowhakaata as they look towards their future as the descendants of
these intrepid and fearless men and wome n. I know the leaders of today are well
equipped with the knowledge needed in today’s world.
May I also take this opportunity to acknowledge ng ā uri o Te Kooti Rikirangi, in this
bill. Over 130 years of stigmatisation has ended for the descendants of Te Kooti.
Finally, families back home in Gisborne and uri around the world have an apology from
the Crown, acknowledging that its actions le d to the deprivation of mana for the
descendants of this great patriot.  His proverbial saying, his whakatauk ī, “E kore he
tangata o Tūranga e kite i a au; e kite he whenua o T ūranga i a au”, has become a song
for the land. It translates as “The people of T ūranga will never see me again; the land of
Tūranga will”. It evokes a new dawn, expressed as a belief that his spiritual return will
occur as this terrible history is laid to rest through the process of legal settlement, which
we are going through now in the 21 st century. The whakatauk ī expresses the hopes of
five generations that land taken at T ūranga will be recognised as having been
wrongfully taken. Then the martyr Te Koo ti Rikirangi—the man who was exiled as a
spy without trial in 1866, without cause—may be able to return home.
Finally, I would like to encourage the hi story of Rongowhakaata that has been
outlined in the Crown acknowledgments and the Crown apologies in this bill—that
Treaty history and these texts, stories, and histories that are a huge contribution to our
4034 Rongowhakaata Claims Se ttlement Bill 26 Jul 2012
national history—I want to encourage our natio n as a whole to grasp the lessons of the
history that is now etched on our statute book. We do not want them to be just sitting on
the shelf. I would like to encourage this Government, or whoever is in Government, that
we make sure that our Treaty history as outlined in these Treaty bills becomes
compulsory teaching in our social studies classes for our tamariki right throughout the
motu. I think it is very important that this hi story is known and that it  is educated to not
only this generation but also generations to come.
May I acknowledge my colleagues in the M āori Affairs Committee, under the chair
of the Hon Tau Henare, and all our fellow members. I also acknowledge the work of
Minister Finlayson and his officials. I am a new member  to this House, and I do think
that in a way we are finishing off the hāngi but it was actually laid down by those before
us. It has the hands of that great states man Sir Michael Cullen and other people and
administrations that have been awhi-ing and tautoko-ing this bill right from the early
days. It is a pleasure to be par ticipating in this third reading and to be part of the select
committee to bring this bill to its final passing.
Finally, I would like to mihi to Rongowha kaata, to Stan Pardoe—I see Lewis up
there—and to all of the kaum ātua and kuia who have travelled all this way. It is a real
honour to mihi and to speak to this bill. I know it is a very important day for you. It
harks back to my own memories, obviously , when I was sitting up there with my
whanaunga from the south, when we were having the passing of our own legislation
down there for Ngāi Tahu. So I know how you must be feeling today: very proud. I join
you and we all join you in  the celebration today. We acknowledge the many, many
years of hard work that you have committed, Stan, and your team there, but also we
acknowledge the many ancestors  who have gone before you. I am very proud to
celebrate this with you today and I mihi to you all. Kia ora tātou katoa.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. E te M āngai o te
Whare, tēnā koe. Tuarua, ki ng ā mema o t ō tātou Whare, t ēnā koutou katoa. Tuatoru, e
mihi atu ki te Wiki o Te Reo M āori, tēnā koutou katoa. Ki a Rongowhakaata, ki ng ā uri
o Te Kooti Rikirangi, tēnā koutou katoa.
[Thank you, Mr Speaker. Greetings to you, Mr Speaker of the House. Secondly, to the
members of our House, greetings to you all. Thirdly, I acknowledge M āori Language
Week, greetings to you all. To Rongowhakaat a and relatives of Te Kooti Rikirangi,
salutations to you all.]
The Green Party is pleased to support th e Rongowhakaata Claims Settlement Bill at
its third reading and to see this bill passed. I want to acknowledge the contribution made
by my colleague Catherine Delahunty in th e second reading. Catherine Delahunty was
resident in this rohe, as she talked about at that time, and has a very strong personal
connection to this area and to the people there. She talked about that personal
experience of being a P ākehā women living in this rohe, knowing these stories and the
hardship that resulted or that was suffered by the mana whenua in these areas.
Those kinds of contributions from, particularly, I think, Pākehā are very important in
this House because it recognises that each pe rson stands to speak and say what their
experience was, and how they ha ve related to those issues in  their life. It acknowledges
that tangata Tiriti have a role in this country  and have a place to st and in this country,
and are as much a part of the history of the process of colonisation as any other. We can,
therefore, take responsibility for our role as a citizen in  a country that has been
colonised and we can acknowle dge the history of hurt that  was caused by the State,
which represents us, by the Government for ces that have represented us, and perhaps
even by our own whānau in some circumstances in the past, not with a sense of guilt but
with a sense of acknowledgment, peace, and justice.
26 Jul 2012 Rongowhakaata Claims Settlement Bill 4035
It is a very important contribution to make. So I appreciate that I have the
opportunity today to speak as a M āori woman, Kahungunu, Āti Hau woman, on this
legislation, and to congratula te Rongowhakaata on all of th eir work in bringing this
legislation into the House, as well as all of those who have spoken before me on this
legislation. Tēnā koutou katoa.
The history of this, of Rongowhakaata, is probably one of the better known histories,
actually. It has been written about in va rious forms because of the extraordinary
personality that was Te Kooti, and the abuse of that history—of th e genuine history of
Te Kooti at this time. It is actually one of the stories that is perh aps one of the better
known, although probably quite badly misrepre sented over time. I agree with my
colleague from Labour who talked about the need  for these stories to  be told in their
fullness and from the mana whenua perspect ive about what happened during that time,
so that the history that our kids have and that  their kids will have is  an honest and true
one, and shows both sides, if you like. It is OK that those stories might be different, but
there are two stories to be told and both are essential.
Twenty-two rangatira of Rongowhakaata si gned the Treaty. They  were invaded by
military forces, Government forces. Member s of Rongowhakaata were killed, a number
were exiled, they were rescued by Te Kooti, and there was retaliation by Te Kooti
against those who were part of that exile process. As a result, the Crown forces came in
very hard on the hap ū and iwi there, capturing the p ā and executing a number of the
prisoners caught in that process. That is set out quite well in the bill and I think it is
good that it is, because again that is a very  explicit description of  the story. But as a
result Rongowhakaata lost virtually all their land and were le ft almost entirely landless.
The titles were individualised—I know we ha ve heard this story repeated a few times
today—so that it became even more difficu lt for Rongowhakaata to retain any kind of
control over their own natural resources.
The settlement process is designed to re turn some kind of co mpensation, some kind
of redress, for the actions of the Crown. As  well, we talk a lot in this House during
Treaty settlements about the generosity of  iwi in accepting these settlements, knowing
that the redress, the compensation, for th e harms caused is just absolutely minute
compared with the harm and the hurt that they have suffered. I want to again
acknowledge that generosity, partly for Rongowhakaata and partly to Rongowhakaata,
because it is actually the rest of the community that needs to understand the extent of
that generosity.
The Green Party has always said, from the time we started here in Parliament with
our parliamentary presence, that the Treaty settlement process wa s not a just one. We
have, without apology, talked during Trea ty settlement debates about the Crown
failures. We consider it part  of our fundamental responsibil ity when we stand up in this
House and talk about Treaty settlements not only to acknowledge the iwi and all of the
work that goes into seeing them come to th e House at this point, but also to hold the
Crown to account for its failures. That is a necessary part of this process, however
uncomfortable, for whichever Government is currently running the country. We said the
same things when Labour was in Govern ment as we say wh en National is in

items.speaker: Government
items.text: the settlement process itself has flaws, and those flaws create undue
hardship for the iwi who in good faith, genuine good faith, are working with the Crown
as best they can to find some redress for their wh ānau, and for their iwi and hap ū, so
that they can move on, at least at this point.
It is important, in our view, as the Gr een Party, that we do hold the Crown to
account, because there are few others who are able to do so, and that is part of our
critical role here in Parliament. To that extent, I feel compelled not only to acknowledge
the importance of the return of the whare in this legislation and what that means for
4036 Rongowhakaata Claims Se ttlement Bill 26 Jul 2012
Rongowhakaata but also to express our re al concern that Rongowhakaata are not
required to carry the burd en of the return of that whare. It is their right and entitlement
to have it back as they see fit, in a way that they see fit, at a time that they see fit. It
remains, in our view, an ongoing obliga tion on the Crown to make sure that
Rongowhakaata have what they need to care for that whare as they se e fit, well into the
future.
This would be a clear demonstration by the Crown of what the Minister was talking
about earlier, which is that it is the actions of the Crown from this point on that will
develop a relationship of trust with Rongowhak aata. It is the actions of the Crown that
count from this point on. One of the actions that the Crown can commit to is to ensure
that Rongowhakaata have everything they need  at every step of the way to make sure
that that whare is returned, and returned in a way that it can be cared for well into the
future. That would be a clear demonstra tion of good faith by the Crown to an ongoing
relationship, in our view.
Finally, I want to acknowledge those who have died during the time of the process of
this settlement to Parliament. As we know , settlements take a long time. People who
work on them often do not see them to fr uition. I acknowledge the work of all those
who will see this settlement  work into the future, and I wish Rongowhakaata and Ng ā
Uri o Te Kooti Rikirangi the best, best wishes for the future. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: T ēnā koe. T ēnā koe. E
ngā maunga Puketapu, Manawar ū, Horouta waka, T ākitimu waka, ng ā uri o Ruapani,
Rongowhakaata, T āmanuhiri, nau mai, hara mai r ā. Hara mai r ā ki Te Whanga-nui-a-
Tara, hara mai r ā ki tēnei Whare Pāremata. E tika ana kia mihi atu ki a t ātau mate, ngā
mea kua mauria e koutou ki r ō Whare nei kia t ū honohono ā tātau mate. Hoki aku
mahara ki a Timi, t ērā Ariki kua tukuna atu, me ō koutou mate, ā tātau mate, n ā reira,
haere koutou okioki pai ma i i te Kaihanga hei wh āriki mā mātau. Nā reira, koutou ki a
koutou ngā mate. Kia hoki ki te kaupapa o te r ā nei, t ēnā koutou, t ēnā koutou, nau mai
rā. He r ā whakahirahira t ēnei, he r ā nui. Kua oti k ē te h īkoi. Rua tekau tau koutou e
kawe ana i tēnei kaupapa mai i te w ā i tīmata ai, i whakatakoto ai t ēnei kerēme ki mua i
te aroaro o te k āwana. Nā reira, kia tangi atu ki a H ēni, ki a Peter Gordon, ki a Darcy.
Nā rā, kai te ora tonu koe Stan, ka whakaaro au, noho tonu. Nā reira, tangi atu ki a rātau
nā rātau i kawe te kaupapa nei.
Ki te kōrero tātau e pā ana ki tēnei kerēme, hoki ngā mahara ki tā koutou hītori, te wā
o te pakanga, te mamae, te taum aha, te whakatorotorotanga o ng ā pā me ērā āhuatanga
muru whenua.
Nā reira, t ēnā koutou, t ēnā koutou, t ēnā koutou kua tae i t ēnei rangi. Ko te w ā
tuatoru, ka p ānuihia t ēnei pepa, pire kei roto i te Whare P āremata nei i te w ā
whakamutunga. Mai i tēnei, ka whakaturetia, mai i tērā ka riro ki a koutou te whakapāha
o te kāwana, ngā taonga me ērā atu ki a koutou. Mōhio anō, ahakoa kua oti tēnā kei roto
tonu i a koutou ngā maumaharatanga ki a rātau kua ngaro atu i ēnei wā, i te pakanga nei.
Nā reira tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou katoa.
Kai te mihi au ki a koutou, Mini ster Finlayson. He tika tana k ōrero, he kaha nei te
haere ki roto i ngā iwi ki te whakatikatika i ngā kerēme.
[Thank you. I welcome you, the mountains Puketapu and Manawar ū, Horouta
canoe, T ākitimu canoe, and the descendants  of Ruapani, Rongowhakaata, and
Tāmanuhiri, welcome, welcome. Welcome indee d, to this Parliame nt House. It is
appropriate that I acknowledge our dead, the on es you brought into this House here to
intermingle with our dead. So my thoughts go back to that high chief, Timi, just
interred, as well as your dead and our dead. Re st well there with the Creator to become
a mat for us. Therefore, rema in there, the dead amongst yo ur own. Allow me to return
to the theme of the day, greetings, acknow ledgments, and welcome indeed. This is an
26 Jul 2012 Rongowhakaata Claims Settlement Bill 4037
important day and a great one. The journey is done. For 20 years you took
responsibility for this matter from the time th is claim began until it was put before the
Government. So I mourn the loss of H ēni, Peter Gordon, and Darcy. However, I note
that you are still alive, Stan, and think to myself, stay alive. So mourn for them, the ones
who took responsibility for this matter.
When we talk about this claim, memories about your history, the period relating to
the battle, the seriousness, setting down redress, and those aspects around land
confiscation will be recalled.
To you who have arrived here today, saluta tions, greetings, and acknowledgments to
you collectively. This is the third reading of this bill, and the final stage in this House of
Parliament. From here it will be passed into law, and from that point, the Government’s
apology with assets, and so on, will become yours. Be mindful of the fact that even
though it has been settled, memories of them who are lost fr om us today as a
consequence of this battle will remain within you. So, I acknowledge and commend you
all.
Acknowledgments, as well, to you and your team, the honourable Minister Chris
Finlayson. What was stated is correct—he moves tirelessly  among the tribes to tidy up
claims.]
I was one who missed out on my holiday, as well, because Minister Finlayson was so
keen to get out amongst the iwi. That is how  quick off the mark he was. In 2005 he was
elected the Minister for Trea ty of Waitangi Negotiations, a nd at the end of the year,
during the Christmas holiday, he spent the whole time going around—up to you and
everywhere else. Kei te mihi au ki a koe e Chris Finlayson me t ō tīma, me ng ā
kaiwhiriwhiri kua tono atu e koe ki roto i ngā iwi o Te Tai Rāwhiti nei.
Nā huri aku k ōrero i n āianei ki ng ā mahi a te Karauna, n ā rātau koutou i t ūkino i te
wā o te pakanga.
[I commend you, Chris Finlayson, your team and negotiators whom you sent in to the
tribes of this East Coast.
My comments turn now to address the actions of the Crown, which was responsible
for these atrocities upon you at the time of the battle.]
In the years 1840 to 1860 Rongowhakaata en joyed a period of peace and economic
development. With the local rivers, fertile soil, and kai moana, Rongowhakaata lived in
abundance, enjoying a measure of prosperity and of trade, and operating several trading
ships. When approached to sell land, they  refused these things and hung on to all of
their rawa, and their lands, and their mana. They refused to sell. What a change was
about to take place in the next decade.
In November 1865 large Crown military forces came to T ūranga, after fighting
Paimarire converts on the East Coast. Th e Crown laid siege to the defensive p ā of
Waerenga a hika, and captured  it in November 1865. At le ast 71 occupants of the p ā
were killed during that assault. The Crow n acknowledges that it used military force
when there was no need to do so, that it  did not pursue all reasonable options for
preserving peace in T ūranga, and that the Crown’s att ack was unwarranted and unjust,
and caused severe and long-term prejudice to Rongowhakaata.
In 1866 the Crown exiled approximately 116 T ūranga men, including Te Kooti
Rikirangi, to the Chatham Islands and we have heard k ōrero about that. They were
detained without trial or conviction for 2 y ears, in harsh conditions, until they escaped
in 1868. The Crown acknowledges that th e indefinite detention of many
Rongowhakaata, including Te Kooti Rikirangi, on the Chatham Islands was an injustice
that deprived them of basic human rights. It  was wrongful, contrary to natural justice,
and impacted not only on the prisoners but on their wh ānau and hap ū who remained in
Tūranga. The Crown also acknowledges that th e unjust treatment of Te Kooti Rikirangi
4038 Rongowhakaata Claims Se ttlement Bill 26 Jul 2012
gave him reason to distrust the Crown when he was offered the chance to return to
Tūranga after his arrival back on the Mainland.
But in 1868 Rongowhakaata were pressured by  the Crown to cede all their lands to
the Crown. This cessation was made under du ress, as the Crown had threatened to
remove all its protection unless the entir e district was ceded. All Rongowhakaata’s
customary interests in their lands were extinguished. By December 1868 Te Kooti
Rikirangi and his followers had retreated to Ngātapa Pā, where they were surrounded by
Crown forces in conjunction with M āori allies. Te Kooti Riki rangi and some of his
followers escaped in early Ja nuary 1869 and were pursued for several days. The Crown
again acknowledges that the Ng ātapa siege and its aftermat h caused the death of many
Rongowhakaata and had a devastating im pact on the iwi a nd the whole of T ūranga. In
subsequent years the Poverty Bay Comm ission and the Native Land Court awarded
individual titles, which only helped the alienation of those titles.
These and other breaches have left Rongow hakaata virtually landless and without
enough resources to meet their present and fu ture needs. The breaches of the Treaty in
the T ūranga area were extremel y significant and have had many lasting effects for
Rongowhakaata, so I would like to take this opportunity to highlight the Crown apology
contained in the deed of settlement and,  subsequently, this Rongowhakaata Claims
Settlement Bill. The apology is significant as it takes a step towards healing the hurt that
is felt as a result of the Treaty br eaches. I would like to refer to t ērā whare rongonui,
ātaahua, kua hangaia i ra ro i a Raharuhi Rukup ō, n ā, ē whakaae ana kia whakahokia
tēnei taonga ki te iwi [ that famous and beautiful house built under the guidance of
Raharuhi Rukupō, and I concur that this treasure be returned to the tribe].
But as with many Treaty settlement redress it ems, there are costs associated with the
return of wāhi tapu or taonga. I am heartened to know that Rongowhakaata do not wish
the return of Te Hau ki T ūranga to create a financial bur den for future generations. As
such, Te Papa Tongarewa will work with R ongowhakaata and the Ministry for Culture
and Heritage to ensure a sustainable future fo r the whare, particularly in relation to its
relocation. This is a significant step towa rds righting the wrongs of the past and
mending the relationship between Rongowhakaata and the Crown.
This bill today also outlines  the redress provided to Ng ā Uri o Te Kooti Rikirangi,
the other claim that we are hearing as well, and I acknowledge  Peter and Maever
Moeau. It acknowledges and is in recognition of the stigmatisation of the descendants of
Te Kooti Rikirangi. This redress includes the vesting of Matawhero Reserve, the
payment of $250,000 for purposes of Te Whare R ākei o Te Kooti Rikirangi, the
payment of $200,000 to Ng ā Uri o Te Kooti Rikirangi, and a relationship with the
Department of Conservation with regard to interpretation material that refers to Te
Kooti Rikirangi. This redress is a significant step towards rehabilitating the reputation
of Te Kooti Rikirangi and acknowledgi ng the discrimination experienced by his
descendants.
The settlement also provides for the establishment of a central leadership group and a
local leadership body. The centr al leadership group has been  established to provide a
forum for Rongowhakaata,  along with other T ūranga iwi—and I think this is pretty
important—to engage with central governme nt departments and ensure that the
principles of the Treaty of Waitangi are being implemented in a coordinated manner
within the Tūranga region. The local leadership body will work with the local council to
contribute to the sustainable management of resources within the Tūranga region. These
redress items provide Rongowha kaata with a valuable oppor tunity to engage with
central and local government on a range of issu es that affect their rohe in the wider
region.
26 Jul 2012 Rongowhakaata Claims Settlement Bill 4039
So tēnā koutou, Noel. Tēnā koutou, Ngai Tāmanuhiri, Rongowhakaata, kua tae katoa
mai koutou i tēnei wā mō tēnei rangi whakahirahira, e tika ana kia mihi atu ki a koutou,
tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou.
[Noel, thank you and your people. Thank you, Ngai Tāmanuhiri and Rongowhakaata,
all of you are here at this point in time in regard to this momentous day. Therefore, it is
fitting that I acknowledge you collectively, greetings and congratulations.]
The settlement redress provided for in this  bill seeks to recogni se the seriousness of
Rongowhakaata grievances and to build a pos itive foundation for futu re generations of
their iwi. I therefore commend this bill to the House. Kia ora.

items.speaker: BRENDAN HORAN
items.text: Ka tangi te t ītī, ka tangi te k ākā, ka tangi hoki
ahau, tihei mauri ora. E ng ā iwi, e ng ā reo, e ng ā mana, e ng ā mātāwaka, tēnā koutou,
tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou katoa. E rau rangatira mā ka mihi atu i runga i te karanga o te
rā, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, tēnā anō tātou katoa.
[The muttonbird calls, the parrot calls, and I call as well, behold th e breath of life.
To the tribes, voices, authorities, and kinship groups, greetings to you, greetings to you,
and greetings to you all. Oh, leaders of a hundredfold, I pay homage to you in respect
of the call of the day, so acknowledgments, salutations, and congratulations once again
to us all.]
I rise on behalf of New Zealand First to acknowledge and support the third reading of
the Rongowhakaata Claims Settlement Bill. I cannot help but wonder; I know the media
is somewhere out there, watching on closed -circuit television, but just imagine if we
were in the States right now. What woul d be happening? Every network would be
screening this, rich histories would be exposed, and movie rights would be bought and
sold. Even in Australia, they would have this all over the networks. But what is going to
lead the news tonight? Is this rich tapestr y, the tragic stories, the amazing day that is
today, the settlement, and the apology going to  lead the news t onight? Or is gay
marriage going to lead the news tonight?

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: What’s wrong with gay marriage?

items.speaker: BRENDAN HORAN
items.text: I feel very sad, and yes, I can understand the Greens saying:
“What is wrong with gay marriage?”. What is wrong is that New Zealand’s history is at
stake here; the knowledge, the healing of New Zealand and New Zealanders—that is
what is at stake. I think it is sad that t onight it probably will not lead the news; that
tonight all of New Zealand will not be listeni ng, will not be hearing about what really
happened, and what a great day today really is.
I agree with the sentiments of many of  the speakers before me—in particular,
Parekura Horomia. The atrocities perpetrated by the Crown on Rongowhakaata are
heinous, and well documented. In 1868 in Ng ā Uri, over a hundr ed Rongowhakaata,
including Te Kooti, were put on boats and ex iled, without trial, to the Chathams. This
took place in the winter months of March to  June. It is somewhat  of a miracle, and
testimony to their prodigious strength, that they  even survived the journey, and then to
escape 2 years later is absolutely phenomenal and amazing.
Around the same time, we must think about the people of Ng ātapa, where a hundred
men were lined up and shot in the head. S hortly after, but stil l in 1868, Te Hau ki
Tūranga was confiscated from Ng āti Kaipoho. For those peopl e who are watching on
television, Te Hau ki T ūranga is a mighty meeting house carved by Raharuhi Rukup ō.
Raharuhi is also the biblical term for Lazar us, and with the imminent return of their
spiritual home, Rongowhakaata look forward to a Lazarus-like return to prosperity in
body, spirit, and mind.
The return of this meeti ng house is paramount, and much  anticipated, and I must
acknowledge the comments made by Minister Finlayson and the hope that he imbibes
those comments. We look forward to that proc ess being dealt with as expeditiously as
4040 Rongowhakaata Claims Se ttlement Bill 26 Jul 2012
possible. We also want to make sure that  the Crown pays for th e insurance as well,
because insurance costs are very high. But the meeting house, the taonga, has also been
plundered over the years, as th e Minister alluded to, with changes being made, and also
over 60 taonga missing from the meeting house.
The hurt, humiliation, atrocities, and terro r inflicted upon Rongowhakaata can never
be fully compensated for, because, after all, who can raise the dead? In financial terms,
one cannot replace what was lost when M āori landowners were dispossessed of their
land, only to watch European farmers lease th at land at peppercorn rates, borrow on the
equity, and build empires, whilst M āori were catapulted into poverty. As with so many
historical grievances, the j ourney to this point has be en extremely hard—taxing,
arduous. So much hard work has been done  by so many people who have passed on. I
would say special praise and acknowledgment to two leadi ng elders of the Gisborne
region who are no longer with us, but no doubt ar e here in spirit. I refer to Darcy Ria
and Hēni Sunderland. We mourn their loss, but celebrate their inspiration, which has led
us to the achievement of this settlem ent and immensely special day. We also
acknowledge and thank the negotiators Stan Pardoe and Jody Wyllie, Meka Whaitiri,
Maever Moeau, and Peter Moeau, and also from the Office of Treaty Settlements
Andrew McConnell and his team. Well done, everyone involved.
We in New Zealand First also celebrate the transparency of the Rongowhakaata
Trust in putting forward their strategic pl an last October. Th e 10 trustees were
democratically elected from five marae, a nd we wish them well in the implementation
of their strategic plan. It is great to see the trustees committing to regular bimonthly
updates through the Rongowhakaata website a nd Facebook. This settlement is long
waited for, and richly deserved. Now, another journey awaits: one of self-determination.
I will leave you with a Maniapoto saying, given to Maniapoto before his journey over to
England to make a plea to Queen Victoria.
Ka hora te marino, kia whakapapa pouna mu te moana, kia tere te k ārohirohi i mua i
tō huarahi. For those who are, agai n, out there and do not understand M āori: may the
calm be widespread, may the ocean glisten like greenstone, and may the shimmer of
many summers dance across your pathway. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: Te mea tuatahi ki a au, ki aku rangatira, t ēnā
koutou, ā, tēnā koutou i haere mai i tēnei rā i runga i te kaupapa o te rā nei, nō reira, nau
mai, haere mai.
[First of all, acknowledgments to you, my leaders who came here today in respect of
the matter of the day, so, salutations and welcome, welcome.]
I suppose I should start off by saying there is  a conflict of inte rest, but I do not
actually see it as a conflict of interest, so I will not. Can I pass on my respects to Stan,
Meka, Jody, Willie, and the team for Rongowhakaata, and everybody else who has been
involved in that side of it.
As I said last week in the second read ing of the Rongowhakaata Claims Settlement
Bill, I find this story to be one of the most  interesting that has not been told in New
Zealand’s history. I want to  give you, if I may, some pa rallels to other happenings
around the world. Around about the same time as the battle of Waere nga a Hika and as
Ngātapa—20 years difference or so after th e battle of Waerenga a Hika and the
slaughter and massacre at Ng ātapa—is one of the world’s better-known massacres, and
that is the massacre at Wounded Knee. I suppos e it brings me to the fact that this
country had better start owni ng its own history. This is not Rongowhakaata’s history;
this is our history—this is New Zealand’s history. We should not refer to it as their
issue; it is our issue. We had better star t teaching this stuff in our schools, because
although to some people “ignorance is bliss”, mo st of the time when there is ignorance
26 Jul 2012 Rongowhakaata Claims Settlement Bill 4041
around, you do not know who you are and you do not know where you are going. And
you certainly do not know where you come from.
There is a whole brilliant history in Rongowhakaata, not only about the sad
occasions. There are happy occasions as well that we need to be telling our mokopuna,
our babies, and ourselves about, like the fact  that Te Kooti was not some layabout who
sat around thinking about how to diddle the Crown out of whatever. He was actually out
there as a business person seeking betterment for his own people. That is a trait that I
think everybody in this House should, and most probably does, stand up and applaud.
About this “deal”, to call it a deal—I suppos e a deal in real terms is when both sides
are getting what they want. You know, you go down to the car market and make a deal
with the guy whom you want to buy a car from. It  is pretty obvious th at this is not that
sort of deal, and that all the power is in the Crown’s hands. But, having said that, the
two sides, if I can use those terms, have come together and decided on a historical
account, some cultural redress, some commercial redress, and some specific research for
Ngā Uri o Te Kooti Rikirangi. I pick up where Minister Finlayson, Minister for Treaty
of Waitangi Negotiations, so eloquently left  off, and that is about Te Hau ki T ūranga.
This is not just about the stealing of a wh are by some Crown agents, because that was
just the start of it. To try to fit it into  the Dominion Museum, they cut most of the
carvings apart. So it is in the light of that ongoing, I suppo se, rape of our culture and
violation of our culture that to see the return of Te Hau ki T ūranga in the most
appropriate manner—and, might I say, maybe as  an arts centre for New Zealand—is I
think, one of the most appropriate parts of this settlement.
For too long M āori have been told they are si ck, dumb, uneducated, and poor. I do
hope that what we do today says to our pe ople especially that you are not sick, dumb,
uneducated, and poor; you are the most brilli ant people this side of the southern
hemisphere, and most probably beyond. I have so much respect and love for our people
that it is not funny. From this day forth I wi ll not ever speak of anything that is bad
about my own, because it is about time that  we patted ourselves on the back, regardless
of the statistics, and said that we are on our way, and we have been for a thousand years.
We should not compare ourselves with P ākehā, Samoans, Chinese, or whoever. We
should compare ourselves with the bright lights of our ow n people. We should compare
ourselves with people like Rukup ō, like Ng ārimu, and like so many of our other
ancestors. I am not going to buy in to any more of the statistics that basically are used to
keep us down and make us feel sad about our selves. There is nothing to be sad about. I
think this occasion and these occasions, as we have started from 9 o’clock this morning,
show that our people are with it, and that they can sit down with the best of them and
negotiate a reasonable deal. I will not say it is a good deal; I will never say it is a good
deal. A good deal would be ha ving it all back. But we know th at that is impossible, and
so this is a reasonable deal.
I want to close by saying what I said and what I will say continually. My message to

items.speaker: Rongowhakaata is this
items.text: beware of companies and shysters b earing good little ideas on
how to spend your money. It is your money, an d it is your settlement. It is for you to
show the way for the rest of us. So pleas e beware of those people out there who knock
on your door and say: “Boy, have I got a deal for you!”. As soon as they say that, shut
the door and make sure you let the dogs loose.
It is fun; I am full of happiness and joy for Rongowhakaata and for M āori that we
can boost ourselves up and we can boost our people up, especially when they deserve
being boosted up. Nō reira e aku mātua, e aku koroua, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, kia ora
mai tātou katoa.
[So to my fathers and elders, greetings, salutations, and acknowledgments to you and
to us all.]
4042 Rongowhakaata Claims Se ttlement Bill 26 Jul 2012

items.speaker: Hon NANAIA MAHUTA
items.text: Tēnā koe, tēnā koutou. E
tāpiri atu aku mihi maioha ki a koutou Rongowhakaata, i pakaru te kaha ki te
whakatutuki i t ēnei kaupapa kei mua i te aroaro i t ēnei wā, nō reira, ki a koutou katoa,
ka nui te mihi atu.
[Thank you, and salutations to you collectively. I add my loving regards to you,
Rongowhakaata, who worked really hard to bring th is matter before us at this point in
time to a conclusion. I acknowledge you greatly.]
It gives me great pleasure to join in the previous comments supporting the legislation
that is about to go through the House today, the Rongowhakaata Claims Settlement Bill.
Having read the historical background in the b ill and also listened to Minister Turia and
my colleague the Hon Parekura Horomia, I will tread lightly on the history of
Rongowhakaata and Ng ā Uri o Te Kooti Rikirangi, lest I tread in the wrong place. So
please do not take my contribution as a dimi nishing of the intent of the legislation,
except to say I recognise in the bill a huge, huge  step forward in terms of the intent of
Rongowhakaata and Ngā Uri o Te Kooti Riki rangi in coming together to work forward
for the betterment of your people and most certainly for future generations.
With that in mind, there are five brief word s in this bill that we should all cherish
when we think about Treaty settlement legislation: “This Act binds the Crown.”
Underpinning those five small words is a deed of settlement with much of the substance
of the intent of Rongowhakaata and Ngā Uri o Te Kooti Rikirangi about what they want
to aspire to. We should always remember that, because this is M āori Language Week,
and when the good people of New Zealand look at  Parliament and listen to the debates,
it is my sincere hope that they do not judge us just on question time. It is my sincere
hope that they believe that we are contribu ting to trying to make New Zealand a better
place, and Treaty settlements are but one of the ways in which New Zealand is
becoming a better place. Why? B ecause it resolves the histori cal injustices of the past.
Why? Because it shows the magnitude and magnanimity of spirit that M āori have had,
despite history, to try to move forward. W hy? Because the Crown, with some level of
humility, recognises that it has a long way to go to rectify the hurt of the past, but also
the necessity of ensuring the durability of settlements despite this.
So to the good people of New Zealand w ho are listening to the debates on Treaty
settlements in the House today, it is my sin cere hope that you see this as a positive step
that can build a nation that is committed to  rectifying history in some small way, to
telling both sides of the story. Part of Rongowhakaata’s bill s eeks to rectify that story.
We often tell the history of ot her iwi very poorly in  this House, and it is often drawn
from what is written in the legislation, but again it is my sincere hope that in the schools
throughout New Zealand—and especially, in this instance, in the Rongowhakaata
region itself, in their schools— they can tell both sides of the story. They were never
ever told to them, their parents, or the pa rents before them. But to their children, yes,
history can be rectified.
I also wanted to comment briefly on the magnanimity of the people of
Rongowhakaata and Ngā Uri o Te Kooti Rikirangi in ced ing much of the varied claims
in their rohe to be able to get to this point. Clause 14 outlines the extent and the nature
of, I guess, the undertakings that had to be sought to be able to come to this point today.
And we should never ever forget that ma ny, many smaller claims have made up the
context of this bigger claim.
It is important because often I have sat on a number of select  committees where
people feel very aggrieved at giving up their own Waitangi Tribunal claim to be able to
join a larger, comprehensive claim—that thei r particular grievances and hurts cannot be
told. So I want to draw the attention of the House to each and every one of those Wai
claims in clause 14, and I want to acknowledge  for the record that it is no small matter
26 Jul 2012 Rongowhakaata Claims Settlement Bill 4043
that iwi have managed to consolidate collecti ve interests of this nature. It is very
significant. It is an important act of goodwill that I, certainly, as a member of this House
want to acknowledge, and I pay tribute to the leadership of those involved in negotiating
the intent of this claim. Much of th e debate has focused on the opportunities for
successful implementation, and again I remind us of those five key words: “This Act
binds the Crown.” It should bind the Crown in every generation that seeks to give life to
the intent of Treaty settlements, but we ha ve to be vigilant. A lthough politicians come
and go, the iwi collectiv e memory is very vivid, and it stays the same, and people will
carry the torch of intent of Treaty settleme nts in ways that we can never fathom or
understand. We have to be diligent as parliamentarians, and, certainly, when you are on
the Treasury benches representing the Crown, implementing the full extent of
undertakings within Treaty settlements. So the cultural redress components are really
important.
Members before me have spoken about the need to return Te Hau ki T ūranga back to
Rongowhakaata, and can I just say this on e thing. Despite the na ture by which this
house has come into the public domain and provenance, I want to acknowledge that this
house has been a huge gift to the nation. For every person who has visited Te Papa
Tongarewa, for every person who has been able to get a glimmer of the richness and the
value of Māori culture and its contribution to shap ing the identity of New Zealand, this
particular whare has played a huge role. So I want to acknowledge that, because it is not
well said and expressed, and I want that recognition to go into Hansard.
The second aspect is really on the implementation of the protocols. Can I just say
that there are a range of protocols here that give body to the opportunities going forward
for the claimant groups. The conservation pr otocol, the Crown minerals protocol, the
fisheries protocol, and the taonga t ūturu protocol—each of those will require the strong
commitment of the Crown’s representatives through age and time to ensure that those
protocols are able to be delivered upon. No matter which administration comes into
force, it is a minimum expectation. This is , I guess, the part of settlements where I
become, I guess, very cautioned—probabl y by our own experience and our own
settlement back home—that unless we as parliamentarians are diligent, for the benefit of
the intent of the Crown, for successful im plementation, then memories will soon fade,
and the intents of these protocols will be lost, and perhaps not as successfully
implemented as is anticipated today.
That is the very reason why I think the statement of the Minister is absolutely
correct. When it comes to Treaty settlements, this small part is a step along the way to a
much greater intent, and that is to see the full realisation of the dreams and aspirations
of Rongowhakaata, Ng ā Uri o Te Kooti Rikirangi realis ed in some very tangible ways,
which the Crown must give body to.
With that small contribution, again I want to commend the bill to the House, and I
am proud that our members of the M āori Affairs Committee have been unwavering and
unstinting in their support of the four bills that have come before us today, and have
shown us that there is a lot to look forward to, especially for the people of
Rongowhakaata, who are no strangers to pr oviding opportunity for their people, for
looking for economic development opportunities, for investing in the future of their next
generation, and, more important, for preparin g themselves well to be able to move
forward successfully.
Nō reira, i raro i t ērā o ng ā tino pitopito k ōrero, ka t āpiri atu aku whakaaro ki ērā i
waihotia i roto i te Whare nei, tēnā koutou katoa.
[So, after that really very brief contributi on, I add my thoughts to those presented by
others in this House, and commend you all.]
4044 Rongowhakaata Claims Se ttlement Bill 26 Jul 2012

items.speaker: LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker, t ēnā koe e te
Whare. Tēnā koutou ng ā iwi rangatira o Rongowhakaata, t ēnā koutou. Ko McGill t ōku
iwi, ko Karapiro taku k āinga, ko Maungatautari taku maunga, ko Waikato te awa. Kei
ahau te rohe pōti o Taupō, ko Louise Upston ahau.
[Thank you, Mr Speaker, and greetings to the House. To the revered people of
Rongowhakaata, salutations and acknowledgments  to you collectively. My clan is
McGill, my home is Karapiro, Maungatautari is my mountain, and Waikato is the river.
I have the Taupō electorate, and my name is Louise Upston.]
I am very proud to speak in the thir d reading of the R ongowhakaata Claims
Settlement Bill. It is fantastic to see so many of you here on this very momentous
occasion. This will be a day that goes down in your history and ours.
One of the words that we use quite a lot wh en we talk about Treaty settlements is the
partnership that is forged between iwi and the Crown. The completion of the legislation
and the completion of the third reading here  today will cement that relationship, that
partnership, in a new way. We also talk about the fact that settlements unlock the
economic potential for iwi, for the region in  which you live, and for the country as a
whole. But I think that, more important, it unlocks the potential of our people, and I use
the word “our” very deliberately because it is your people and ours who will benefit
from the history that is made here today.
Some of my colleagues have spoken at length in summary of your settlement so I do
not want to traverse that in too much detail, ot her than just to be very present to the fact
that the Waitangi Tribunal has described the Treaty breaches arising from the Crown
military action against the T ūranga iwi as some of the worst in our history. That is part
of our history that none of us should be pr oud of. But I think it is also important to
acknowledge that it is part of our history. The settlement includes the historical account
and the Crown acknowledgments, which form  the basis for the Crown apology to
Rongowhakaata, and that is what  I want to just spend a bit of time on today in this
House. On 1 October 2011 the Treaty set tlements Minister, the Hon Christopher
Finlayson, delivered the extensive apology for the Crown’s conduct in the 1860s, which
included the operation of the Poverty Bay Commission and the execution of between 86
and 128 unarmed prisoners at Ngātapa pā.
I was not present, as some of my colle agues were, when th at Crown apology was
delivered, but I was present for the Crown a pology to Raukawa. Raukawa is an iwi in
the Taupō electorate. I wondered if I could have  your indulgence for a moment to share
with you my experience of being present at  that Crown apology. My memories of that
day will be for ever etched as part of my history, because it showed me a whole
different level of partnership and what is possible—from the p ōwhiri and through the
speeches, tears literally fell upon the ground at the memory of the history and the stories
that were told of the challenges of the negot iation, of the many hours of effort that went
on, and of the passing of thos e who were then not presen t on the day that the Crown
apology was delivered. It was no surprise to me that day, for the Raukawa apology, that
also the rain fell from  the sky. To me that was the tear s and the rain pl aying a part in
cleansing some of that pain. I just feel so immensely privileged to  have experienced a
Crown apology. And I was immensely proud of  Minister Finlayson. Some would say
that that was the delivery of  words of a speech, but I can promise to those of you who
are listening, who may have never had the experience of witnessing a Crown apology, it
is a moment to behold, and it is part of our history.
I am sorry to those here from Rongowhak aata that I personally was not present for
your apology, but I can believe what was in your heart and y our minds and your soul as
you heard that apology. That is what we bring to this House on this occasion in the third
reading of your settlement bill. The thing that was very present was aroha. I think that is
26 Jul 2012 Rongowhakaata Claims Settlement Bill 4045
the essence of partnership. When we talk about Treaty settlements being a partnership
between iwi and the Crown, that is where a new beginning is possible, that is where that
potential gets to be unlocked. It is exciting to be here today.
Earlier today in the two bill s that have gone before, I ha ve talked about making sure
that we share the stories. Y ou are very good at sharing yo ur stories—far better than
some of the rest of us are. So part of the story is to l ook at the new chapter and the new
story. Perhaps it is a book or  even a trilogy—tril ogies are in these days. Perhaps what
we should instead be focusing on is what comes next. And I look forward to hearing
more of Rongowhakaata and where you take this day.
I am very proud to speak in this reading, to speak of the partnership between Crown
and the iwi. In recognition of Te Wiki o Te Reo Māori, I hope we can imprint this in Te
Reo as well as English to make sure that  this moment in history—this moment in
time—lasts for many more of us, for our ch ildren, and for our gr andchildren. It is
fantastic to see tamariki in the gallery to witness this mome nt. Congratulations. N ō
reira, tēnā koutou.

items.speaker: CHARLES CHAUVEL
items.text: It is an honour to take a call in this debate, and,
in particular, to follow my colleagues on this side of the House the Hon Nanaia Mahuta,
the Hon Parekura Horomia, and Rino Tirikate ne, because I want to associate myself
with the remarks that they have made already in this debate.
Next Wednesday I will have been a member of this House for 6 years, but I have not
asked to participate in a Treaty settlement  debate until now. My conversation with my
colleague Parekura Horomia earlier this afternoo n led us to agree that I should do so on
this occasion, as shadow Attorney-General , because, as many people in the gallery
know, I am a person who was born and spent the first two decades of his life in the rohe
of Rongowhakaata. My family and I experien ced the great generos ity of the tangata
whenua of that part of our country while we  were living in that part of New Zealand. I
wish to add my personal words of tribute, gratitude, and acknowledgment to those who
have already spoken in the debate today.
My mother’s family arrived in Gisborne as immigrants from Scotland in the 1940s.
My father came to Gisborne a little bit late r. He came to New Zealand to go to school.
He came to Gisborne to practice law. He did some work for a number of people whom I
see present today, helping them with their la nd and estate work before it was an area of
practice that was popular, or in vogue. He was very proud of the work that he did. In the
1970s and 1980s my sister and I went to school in your rohe.
As I mentioned earlier, the generosity that my  family and I, as manuhiri to that rohe,
experienced is always something that strikes me when I look back on my childhood, and
when we contemplate the context of the set tlement debate today we realise just how
extraordinary that generosity is. That is fo r at least two reasons. One is the fact that
yours is one of the most blood -drenched episodes in our co lonial history. I will not
repeat the accounts that have been recounted ea rlier in the debates of the atrocities that
your ancestors had to put up with at the hands  of the Crown. But there is something that
I think is even worse than the fact that those atrocities took place: it is the fact that many
of us—most of us, all of us—who went th rough the New Zealand education system in
the 1970s and 1980s were not taught about them . So another important thing about this
process is that we can record our history. N obody will have the excuse to say that they
do not know about it, because all that history is  now going to be recorded for ever in an
Act of this Parliament and in the settlement  documentation, and that is absolutely as it
should be. Earlier speakers are correct—we do not teach our history properly. And if we
do not teach our history properly, we cannot expect people to understand and appreciate
the generosity that is being shown today by the fact that Rongow hakaata are accepting
the settlement that we are now enacting.
4046 Rongowhakaata Claims Se ttlement Bill 26 Jul 2012
I have spoken about generosity several times  in this call. It has always been on
display by Rongowhakaata. The redress that they will rece ive under this settlement, as
with all Treaty settlements—and this an observation I think made many years ago now
by the Hon Mark Burton—will never compensate the iwi for what it experienced from
1865 onwards. Never in a Treaty settlement is there adequate redress or compensation
for the wrongs of the past. So it is very much always an act of generosity on the part of
the Treaty partner to accept what is proffe red by the Crown in a binding settlement. We
are fortunate today that this Treaty settlement has been accepted and is being enacted.
I think we are also very fortunate that the generosity that I mention has, in a
somewhat rare occasion in this House, proved contagious. My colleagues earlier
acknowledged the work that has been done by the Minister for Treaty of Waitangi
Negotiations in progressing this and other Treaty settlements, and I join with them in
acknowledging that work.
The Minister in turn has very properl y acknowledged anothe r truth about the
settlement process: it does not exist just in the present. The negotiators on both sides
stand on the shoulders of giants, and they rely on the work that was done in the past in
order to bring the settlement about. For the part of the Crown, the Minister properly
acknowledged the work that was done by the Hon Michael Cullen as Deputy Prime
Minister in the previous administration. The signing in principle on behalf of the Crown
of the agreement for a colle ctive settlement package in August 2008 was what enabled
the detailed negotiations to o ccur and to progress to the point that they have today. The
historical research that was done in order to back up the Treaty claim that was processed
through the Waitangi Tribunal in the early part of the last decade was able to be done
and resourced only because the fourth Labour  Government had amended the Treaty of
Waitangi Act in 1985 to allow for grievances back to 1840 to be heard and determined
by the tribunal, and for historical research and advocacy services to be resourced as part
of that process.
Thank goodness that that happened, because that  is how we were able to come to a
definitive recording of the history that has been spoken about by previous speakers and
will be recorded in the deed and in the Act of Parliament. It is a timely reminder that the
Treaty process needs to continue to be resourced adequately. This applies to the tribunal
and to those who present claims before it. It is no good to have a deadline for the cut-off
of Treaty settlements if the process is not properly resourced by the Crown in all
respects, and we should all remember that in  this House when we speak in support of
Treaty settlements such as the one that is being debated today.
It is an honour to have had an opportunity to  speak in this debate. I want to conclude
by again acknowledging the tremendous genero sity of Rongowhakaata. I have been a
beneficiary of it personally, so I know that the people in the gallery will not be worried
at all about what leads the One News tonight. You have more important concerns than
that, given the long time that it has taken, the long wait, for justice to be brought to you.
To Rongowhakaata and to Ngai Tāmanuhiri—because I am not sure whether I will have
the opportunity to speak in the next debate—I want to say th at it is a marvellous thing
that the generosity that you have shown is now being shown to the nation as a whole.
Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: Tihei mauri ora.
Whakataka te hau ki te uru, whak ataka te hau ki te tonga. Kia m ākinakina ki uta, kia
mātaratara ki tai. E hī ake ana te atākura, he tio, he huka, he hauhunga. T ēnā koutou. Ki
te Whare e t ū nei, t ēnā koe, ki a Papat ūānuku kei waho, t ēnā koe. Ki ng ā mate, haere,
haere, haere. Ki ngā tangata, rangatira, kaumātua o Rongowhakaata, tēnā koutou. Ki ngā
mema o te P āremata, tēnā koutou. Ki a koe te Kaik ōrero hoki, t ēnā koe. T ēnā koutou,
tēnā koutou, tēnā tātou katoa.
26 Jul 2012 Rongowhakaata Claims Settlement Bill 4047
[Behold the sneeze of life. Ce ase the winds from the west , cease the winds from the
south. Let the breezes blow over the land, le t the breezes blow o ver the ocean. Let the
red-tipped dawn come with a sharpened air,  a touch of frost, and a promise of a
glorious day. Greetings to you collectively, greetings to the Hous e standing before us,
and greetings to Mother Earth outside. Depart the deaths, depart, farewell.
Acknowledgments to you, the leaders and elder folk of Rongowhakaata, to the members
of Parliament, and to the Speaker, as we ll, greetings. So greetings, greetings, and
greetings to us all collectively.]
Well, kia ora, everybody. It is  a real privilege to stand in the House at this third
reading of the Rongowhakaata Claims Settleme nt Bill. I firstly acknowledge the work
of members of Parliament across the House, le d by the Hon Chris Finlayson, who has
done an outstanding job, I believe, for this nati on over the last 3 years. He continues in
this term of Government to work tireless ly to bring about settlements throughout our
nation.
Just 2 weeks ago I was in the Chatham Isla nds with the Minister, and he took me out
to Pitt Island, where he is working on a se ttlement with Moriori out on Pitt. He shows
his passion for this drive by goi ng to the outermost islands of  our country to make this
happen. He has demonstrated that through some  22 deeds of settlement that have been
brought to the House in the last 4 years, which is absolutely fantastic.
But let us not dwel l on those settlements; today is about the Rongowhakaata
settlement. I do not want to dwell on what other members have sai d. Clearly, your iwi,
your hap ū had to go through unbelievable events in this country, in ou r history. I am
proud, as the member from Heretaunga—fro m Hawke’s Bay—just down the road from
“Gizzy”, to be able to stand in  this House, to be part of the settlement process, and to
acknowledge what took place hi storically and what we are now doing to reconcile, to
see apologies made, and for some form of redress to be made going forward.
I will talk just briefly about that redress, and also touch on what my colleague across
the House said about our history and how impo rtant I believe it is that it is taught in
schools going forward, because it was not some thing that Charles or I were taught. I
think, particularly locally, I am encourag ing my children to understand what happened,
certainly in Ahuriri and Heretaunga, and I th ink there is an obligation further up, in
Gisborne, for schools up there to understand what happened at Ngātapa Pā. Clearly, it is
something that for all of us is not a fine time in our history—that is for sure.
The whakataukī I used at the start of my speech—my whaik ōrero—today talks about
a new dawn, a touch of frost, the commencemen t of a glorious new era. I guess that is
essentially what we are trying to achieve. We are not going to  solve all of the issues or
be able to address everything, but I think this is an outst anding effort by the Crown and
iwi to come together in a partnership and to  go forward. In that regard, I encourage you
as an iwi to make the very most of th is opportunity. I think there are wonderful
opportunities to be able to b ecome even more a part of the Poverty Bay economic base
up there, and to drive real change as a result of this settlement.
Without any further ado, it is a privileg e to be here, and I acknowledge once again
Mr Finlayson, members across the House w ho have played a role in this, and
particularly the iwi, who are here today. I will close by repeating that whakatauk ī,
because this is a new era, a new dawn for Rongowhakaata.
Whakataka te hau ki te uru, whak ataka te hau ki te tonga. Kia m ākinakina ki uta, kia
mātaratara ki tai. E hī ake ana te atākura, he tio, he huka, he hauhunga.
[Cease the winds from the west, cease the wi nds from the south. Let the breezes blow
over the land, let the breezes blow over the ocean. Let the red-tipped dawn come with a
sharpened air, a touch of frost, and a promise of a glorious day.]
Bill read a third time.
4048 Rongowhakaata Claims Se ttlement Bill 26 Jul 2012
Waiata
Karanga

items.speaker: Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations
items.text: I move, That the Ngai T āmanuhiri Claims
Settlement Bill be now read a third time . E rau rangatira m ā, tēnei te mi’i ki a koutou i
runga i te kaupapa o te r ā. Tēnā koutou ng ā rangatira o Ngai T āmanuhiri, kātahi anō te
Whare Pāremata nei kia w’akanui i te pire nei. He h ōnore mōku kia tū hei kaikōrero mō
tēnei, te pānuitanga mutunga o te pire. Tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou katoa.
[I greet you, leaders of a hundredfold, in respect of the matter of the day. Salutations
to you, the leaders of Ngai T āmanuhiri. This Parliament House has at last celebrated
this bill, which I deem it an honour to speak to in this, its final reading.
Acknowledgments, salutations, and congratulations to you all.]
The Ngai T āmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bill will settle finally the historical Treaty
of Waitangi claims of Ngai T āmanuhiri. The third reading of this bill brings to an end a
day of great sadness and loss as the enduring memories of descendants have resonated
throughout this Chamber. We have wept w ith them as we have traversed over the
history we share. The loss extends beyond th e tribal boundaries to also reflect on the
health of our nationhood. The settlement stories have impacted on the rule of law, the
definition of just and good settlement, and the protection of M āori mana motuhake. In
all these principles and the failures of the Cr own to live up to that ideal, it goes to the
surface of our capacity to live up to the prom ise of the Treaty. These settlement bills,
therefore, become a benchmark for all New Zealanders to assess the progress that we
have achieved since the signing of Te Tiriti o Waitangi in 1840.
Ngai Tāmanuhiri’s settlement part stretches back 20 years. Today those in the public
gallery and all of us below reflect on those who are not with us, those who have worked
tirelessly on Ngai T āmanuhiri’s claims and who are not here to witness this day. The
rohe that forms the home of Ngai T āmanuhiri extends from K ōpututea, down the
coastline over Wharerata Forest to Parit ū, and from Parit ū the area extends inland
towards Lake Waikaremoana. It  is a beautiful pa rt of the world, an exquisite tribal
sanctuary.
Up until 1865 Ngai T āmanuhiri had full control of th eir lands and resources. The
people were participating su ccessfully in the New Zeal and economy and, indeed, the
sun shone brightly for the people of this eastern coast. When war broke out in other
regions Ngai Tāmanuhiri remained neutral, including when fighting came close to home
in 1865. Into this peaceful haven, then, the Crown’s attack on Waerenga a Hika is
inexplicable. There was no need to use military force in T ūranga. The military forces
took part in indiscriminate looting. Those attacks contribut ed to acute food shortages,
which in themselves caused loss of life. On top of that, the dete ntion of some Ngai
Tāmanuhiri on Wharekauri inflicted unwarranted hardship on them and their w’anau. It
was wrongful, it was unwarranted, it was unjust, it was a breach of natural justice, and it
was a breach of Te Tiriti o Waitangi. Well over a century later, in 1992, Eric John Tūpai
Ruru, Tūtekawa Wyllie, and Peter Gordon lodged a claim with the Waitangi Tribunal
on behalf of Te Aitanga-a-M āhaki, Ngai T āmanuhiri, and Rongowha kaata, referred to
as Wai 283.
The Minister in an earlier speech referred to settlements as going to the very heart of
our nation, and it is in the process of telli ng our stories, documenting our truths, and
outlining our experience that we come anywhe re close to the prospect of reconciliation.
The Crown’s relation with Ngai T āmanuhiri has involved some of the darkest episodes
26 Jul 2012 Ngai Tāmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bill 4049
in the country’s history, and that sense of grief and loss su ffered by, and the impact on,
this iwi remains with us all, but more par ticularly so, of course, for the iwi, who are
represented here today. It is a tragic tale of mass executio ns, of land loss, and of the
extinguishment of customary interests, leading to the erosion of Ngai T āmanuhiri’s
traditional tribal structures. As a direct consequence Ngai T āmanuhiri have lived with
poorer housing, lower educationa l achievements, and worse h ealth than any other New
Zealanders, yet, despite this painful history, they have made a significant contribution to
the wealth and development of the nation, and have at all times graciously honoured
their Treaty obligations and responsibilities.
In particular, the settlement pays tribute to Ngai T āmanuhiri’s contribution to the
defence of the nation. Knowing even as little as we do of the injustices that this iwi have
suffered at the hands of the Crown, we cannot help but be overwhelmed by the spirit of
generosity that they have shown the nation in having faith in wo rking with the Crown
on this settlement.
I want to be very clear for the record th at in this settlement today, the Crown is
deeply sorry that it has failed until now to address the injustices in an appropriate
manner. The Crown sincerely apologises fo r its many failures to respect Ngai
Tāmanuhiri mana and to protect them fr om being left virtually landless and
economically marginalised. We all hope that  this settlement will provide a foundation
for this tribe and the Crown to move forward in a spirit of coopera tion, mutual benefit,
and trust.
I move, therefore, to some of the detail in  the deed of settleme nt signed in March
2011 by the Hon Chris Finlayson with N ā Rongowhakaata Raihania and Hope Ng ā
Taare T ūpara as trustees of the T āmanuhiri Tutu Poroporo Tr ust. The settlement
facilitates the transfer of Young Nick’s H ead National Historic Reserve, and endorses
the name change to Te Kuri a Paoa. It will enable Ngai T āmanuhiri to purchase Te
Wherowhero Lagoon. They will be a 50 percen t shareholder in the Wharerata Forest.
There is funding for cultural revitalisation,  and there is a clear commitment to
relationship redress with Crown agencies.
It was pleasing to see a letter from Mayor Meng Foon stating that the council is keen
to help advance and support the mana motuhake of Ngai T āmanuhiri, recognising that
the flow-on benefits will also  extend to all of Te Tai R āwhiti. I want to extend those
flow-on benefits wider across the land, because  we all benefit from these settlements,
both Māori and Pākehā alike.
The Crown apology in the legislation states  that “The Crown seeks to restore its
honour and reputation as a Treaty partner and atone for its pa st failures to uphold” Te
Tiriti o Waitangi. As part of th e journey moving forward, Ngai T āmanuhiri are working
with other T ūranga iwi to establish a memorial to  commemorate members of those iwi
who lost their lives at the ha nds of the Crown. It will provide a sombre reminder to all
of Aotearoa of the history that has shaped our sense of selves.
I want to conclude this today with a w’akataukī that the Waitangi Tribunal used in its
report Turanga Tangata Turanga Whenua : “W’akamoea ngā maunga, kia w’ ānau ko te
pai.”—only good can result when great mountains  are joined. How can we as a country
come together and bring our shared aspira tions for Treaty justice? How do tangata
whenua and tangata Tiriti work in the spirit of collaboration to bu ild a strong basis for
nationhood? The constitutional review that has taken place is but one opportunity. It is a
very important concept for all of us to ponder. Tēnā tātou katoa.

items.speaker: Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA
items.text: Tēnā koe. Te pai o te
rangi nei e te Kaiwhakahaere o te Whare nei, ko te tae tata atu t ātau ki te otinga o te
hīkoi roroa atu o t ēnei rangi. I a koutou o te hau k āinga, Tāmanuhiri, e mihi kau ana,
tēnā koutou. E tae kaha atu koutou tata ana ki o whanaunga tata ki te w āhi nei o te
4050 Ngai T āmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bill 26 Jul 2012
Whare Mīere, te wāhi e mahi atu ng ā tangata o te Karauna ki a koutou. E tautokotia atu
ngā whakaaro o te tuahine a T āriana, ko te tukuna o te whenua, ko te t āhae hoki o te
katoa o te whenua ā koutou mai i te Karauna. N ō reira tēnā koutou. E te matua Noel, e
mihi kau ana ki a koe, ki a r ātou i roto i tō tātou rōpū kaha, rua tekau ma waru, t ēnā koe
mō tēnā. Mai i t ō haerenga mai i Muriwai, tae atu ki  te pakanga, hoki ora atu ki te
kāinga, i konei kē koe tēnā koe mō tēnā.
I a koutou ng ā mea pakeke o te k āinga, e rongo atu t ātou, e kite atu t ātou i te mahi i
roto i a T āmanuhiri, i a Rongowhakaata, ōrite atu ki a koutou, e m ōhio atu koutou i te
mamae, ngā nawe e puta ana mai i te mahi o ng ā hōia, nō reira t ēnā koutou n ā te mea,
he nui atu ng ā whakaaro i roto i a t ātou mō te mahi kino i a T āmanuhiri, he mahi kino,
he mahi taurekareka, tera ano te mahi ki a ratou ēngari, e kaha ana r ātou hei ora atu, n ō
reira tēnā tātou. E te tuahine, e Tariana, kia kaha.
[Thank you. The good thing about this day, Mr Speaker of this House, is that the long
journey to this day is nearly  over. To you, the locals, Ng āi Tāmanuhiri, I acknowledge
you in your efforts to get here in respect of  your close relationships to this place, the
Beehive, where people of the Crown work with you. I endorse the views of fellow
colleague Tariana in respect of how land is offered and how all your lands were also
stolen by the Crown. So congr atulations. To you, the elde r Noel, I acknowledge you,
and them as well, in that mighty group of ours, the 28th Battalion. Congratulations on
your involvement. You came from Muriwai, went to war, returned home alive, and here
you are now. I commend you.
To all you elders of home, we heard and saw what happened to the people of Ng āi
Tāmanuhiri and Rongowhakaata. It was the same with you. You experienced the pain
and concerns that resulted from  the actions of the soldiers, so I salute  you all, because
we have many views about the atrocities experienced by T āmanuhiri—it was bad stuff,
it was belittling, but they were resilient and survived these ordeals, so I acknowledge us
all. Be resolute, sister colleague Tariana.]
Nā te mea, because this is my last chance to talk toda y from this side, I thought I
would embellish, understanding that my relations from Ngai T āmanuhiri will always
have my support and our support. I wa nt to mihi to my whanaunga N ā Rongowhakaata
Raihānia, and everybody else up there. Kia ora koutou. He was 50 the other day. He
looks like Tau Henare. Kia ora tātou. Happy birthday.
As Minister Turia pointed out, to cede all of their land th rough ungracious actions of
the Crown is something that makes the mind boggle. I mean, just imagine half these
dairy farmers losing their land today. That is  what we should do as a Crown: take their
land off them. What is wrong with that, Mr Fi nlayson? Take half the farms away from
them; give those farms to the Chinese. Take those farms off them and give them to these
people. That is exactly what happened here. Th at is the reality. That is what happened.
They took the land off them. They had no say.  If you have ever be en to Muriwai, my
cousin Fuchsia went over there and lived there. I am not too sure what she was doing
there, but she always said it  was paradise. If you go to Mu riwai they have still got the
old trees growing, their whare is strong, they  feed you like billy-o, and they are great
people. They are great people. Barney Whaitiri always said that the water that laps here
will always sustain us, like our whakapapa did. Those people have passed on—a lot of
them—Toko and all of those kaumātua who are not here today. But they have seen fit to
come down here.
I want to talk over a couple of the issues in  relation to the settlement. I see there is a
Crown mineral protocol in this function, I sa y to the Minister of  Treaty of Waitangi
Negotiations—very interesting. I hope they strike gold.
