items.text: But the Greens say no.

items.speaker: Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA
items.text: I do not care what the Gr eens think or you think; I
hope they strike whatever and that it is put in  real context, that it is not given to them
and then taken away. The Minister knows I have been on his case for a fair while. He is
going to end up a sir, I think, some time. Bu t, you know, all these Government agencies
and these protocols—whether it is Work and Income or Child, Youth and Family or the
Department of Conservation, which is in here. The Department of Conservation is
always in here. I found it very interesting. When you get to the summary, what does it
say? I will read you what it says: “Is there any private land being transferred? No. …
Are the public’s rights affected? No. … What are Statut ory Acknowledgments?”. There
are not too many of them, but they are relevant to the Resource Management Act. There
are a lot of noes in here from a group of people who never even had an answer—yes or
no—and took everything. The deed of settlement is $11.07 million plus interest, and the
value of the cultural redress is getting there.
I think that with this claim, building on what the Minister for Wh ānau Ora, Tariana
Turia, said, there has to be more than just a sign-off. As Tau Henare said, let us get on
with the business. This puts ri ght a terrible wrong, and for me it is a wonderful day to
celebrate. That is why I want this. There is no t one of those monsters up there, and they
will most probably see me on TV. You are not  supposed to say anything bad about the
press. It makes me bloody sick that all they are talking about is M āori being mad, bad,
and sad, and Tau Henare smoking. We are a lot better than that—yes, we are. M āori is a
lot smarter than that. These people have stood the worst of the wors t, in the sense of
losing all their lands, and they go home.
The irony is that when the coloniser came, and that little, short P ākehā fella, or
British fella, jumped up and said: “Land ahoy! ”, it was the first place in New Zealand
they saw. You would not believe it, the way th ey have been treated. I say that seriously,
not because they are here but because we n eed to be reminded about that, and that it
needs to be talked about. I know that the tw o Ministers sitting over there, the Minister
for Wh ānau Ora and the Minister for Treaty of  Waitangi Negotiations, were listening
intently and bring some real credence to th ese partnerships, and th at is one thing the
Minister and I agree on. It is no good writing out  these protocols and these charters that
say: “Be kind to them, DOC. Be good to them, LINZ. Be kind to them, TPK.”, and have
nothing come of it. That is what seems to be happening. So, Minister Finlayson, again, I
would encourage you to keep an eye on it . If you do not want to  use Tariana or
somebody else, you get me. I will keep an eye on it for you. What happens in the
continuation is a serious part of progress.
The sums here, as much as they have agreed  to them, are but a pittance in relation to
what was done. The land deal in relation to the forestry—that they get 50 percent and 50
percent is kept—is another issue. I am glad that the funds go with it, but even in the
sense of giving them the forestry and the purchase requirements, just from my quick
reading, it seems to be a bit rich. I want to say that again, Minister, and I have been
professing and offering you a whole lot of support.
Here is a very important one, because we ain’t quite there yet in finalising this. I
notice in there that Young Nick’s Head is renamed Te Kur ī a Paoa / Young Nick’s
Head. It has been like that for 100-odd-pl us bloody years as Young Nick’s Head. Why
not get rid of it and name it Te Kur ī a Paoa? What is this “slash” business? I do not
know whether iwi agreed to it or not, but se riously, what is that about? I have brought
that up before—“Te Kur ī a Paoa / Keep Everybody Else  Happy / Young Nick’s Head”.
Rubbish! I know the Minister agrees with me. Chris Finl ayson does not really care
about that. But it is right.
4052 Ngai T āmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bill 26 Jul 2012
You know, everybody wants to talk about young K āhui, and that is a dastardly, ugly
deed: he patu w āhine, he patu tangata [ killing women and men ]. No doubt about it. We
participate in that and so do P ākehā. But the way it carries on in the press is that that is
all we are—mad, bad, and sad. [ Bell rung] Mr Speaker, you can ring the bell all you
like, but I will tell you this. I do not want to leave here today knowing what will happen,
and what has happened in a whole lot of ot her settlements. They have said: “We signed
a charter with them. We signed a fisherie s charter. We signed a Crown minerals
charter.”, and nothing, t ītoi, nothing out of it—nothing. That is a fact. I trust you,
Minister, to do the right thing.
That thing about that sewage—these are th e people who get it. That water laps on
them. But I have to say it is a damn ir ony, after 150-odd years. I was privileged enough
to go up to the signing at the reserve. Like I said, I wanted to walk but they put me in a
helicopter with the Minister and we got up there. I was privileged to be there. There was
a conservationist American who got the land, at the end of the day. But at the end of the
day this is not about keeping the other pe ople happy; this is about putting something
right that was terribly wrong in  this country, and, certainly, we should be better than
that as politicians and not just rise up when M āoris break a window in a shop or piss
against a wall, or something like that, because that is what makes the news.
At the end of the day, I would certainly want to suggest strongly that Ngai
Tāmanuhiri are given every support as they go through. The deal is the deal—great.
Whether it is the land they have got to purchase, the forestry shares, or whatever else,
they need a lot of help—ongoing help. It is not too easy to understand that the costs
shoot up. There were no costs to the pe ople who took them. They  took it, and they
created wealth out of it. There has been no analysis of that. It is really critical, in my
mind at least, that we send them away understanding that they will be supported and
cherished. Kia ora tātou. Tērā anō te mea i roto i āku mō te rangi nei.
[So acknowledgments to us. That is what I have in me about this day.]
It has been a great day for Māori to celebrate. On the Māori calendar it is supposed to
be a good day for fishing and a good day for getting k ūmara ready for this party season.
But this day should be remembered as th e one when we did these four Treaty
settlements together, and we got a thing put right, as well as we could as politicians, and
it is something we should celebrate. Do not  give me this nationhood building thing and
not show up to support it. Kia ora tātou. Thank you.
Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON (Minister for Treaty of Waitangi
Negotiations): T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker, and t ēnā koutou to our guests in the gallery.
Parekura Horomia has done that to me all day. He has upstaged me right throughout the
course of the debate, but always, as you know with Mr Horomia, for the best of reasons.
I really welcome all those who are in the gallery—those of you who have travelled from
Tūranga-nui-a-Kiwa to join us on this very important occasion. I especially recognise
that great rangatira, Nolan Raih ānia, whose immense contribution to our country,
through his service in the 28 th Māori Battalion, I greatly admire . I see him grinning up
there. He gets very embarrassed when I men tion him, but he deserves all the accolades
that he receives, because he is a great New Zealander.
As is very clear, this bill, the Ngai T āmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bill, settles the
historic grievances of this iwi. The Crown acknowledges and formally apologises for its
breaches of the Treaty of Waitangi, offers an apology, and there are various forms of
redress, which Mrs Turia has mentioned and I am not going to repeat them in my
speech. But this day has indeed been a long time coming. The claims were first made to
the Waitangi Tribunal 20 years ago, in 1992. The claims were inquired into by the
tribunal, and it reported in 2004. It is well established that the grievances that it found,
the breaches of the Treaty, were  very serious indeed. Ngai T āmanuhiri entered
26 Jul 2012 Ngai Tāmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bill 4053
negotiations with the Cr own in 2005, as part of  the collective of T ūranga-nui-a-Kiwa
iwi, and in September 2008 signed the agreement in principle.
It is one of those unfortunate  things that from the agreement in principle to deed of
settlement, the journey is sometimes very long, because in the deed of settlement all the
details have to be finalised, whereas in the agreement in principle, it can be a fairly
generalised document. There has been a lo t of work—an enormous amount of work—
between September 2008 and March 2011. It was a wonderful day, a Saturday morning,
when Mr Horomia and I and other officials— Mrs Turia was there as well—were at that
beautiful marae south of Gisborne, Muriwai Ma rae, to sign the deed of settlement. As
Mr Horomia said, it was a very special day, because we began it by helicoptering up to
the top of the point and initialling the deed  of settlement, and then we came down, and
the actual signing was on the marae.
As I said in my second reading speech last week, it was the first time I had ever done
it as Minister for Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations, but I read out the full
acknowledgement and the apology. One was awar e that it was a very eerie sort of
feeling in the grounds of the marae. I said  to Mrs Turia: “What is going on?” and she
said people were weeping. Th at is perhaps why I get very angry when I hear people
diminish these settlements as mere “deals”, in some kind of superc ilious manner. They
are anything but deals; they are very important acts that we enter into—that the Crown
and iwi enter into—in order to resolve these ma tters that plague our past, so that we can
get on with life. It was a very special day, a nd I want to thank, publicly, the iwi for that
day and for the way in which they have negotiated with me over the last 4 years.
In this settlement, as I said, the Crown acknowledges a number of breaches. Some
mention, in the context of Rongowhakaata, was made by Mr Tirikatene about the men
not being tried in accordance w ith the standards of justice that people were  entitled to,
and then they were imprisone d in harsh conditions on th e Chatham Islands for more
than 2 years. Mr Tirikatene marvelled at how the good men of Rongowhakaata managed
to escape, and the same principle applies to Ngai T āmanuhuri. I have to say that I still
marvel at it myself. I was over in the Chathams a few weeks ago, and Mr Tremain and I
jumped in a crayfish boat to go down from Ōwenga on the south coast of the Chatham
Island over to Pitt Island. It is fair to say—and it was a reasonably pleasant day—that
the journey could be described as interesting. So I have no do ubt at all that the courage
and the determination of those men of Ngai T āmanuhuri to get back to T ūranga-nui-a-
Kiwa was truly, truly impressive.
The other breach that I particularly want to refer to is the act of the Crown in
returning land, and then promoting legislation that basically gave ownership of the land
to individuals rather than to the collective, undermining the ability of the iwi to maintain
its property. That is why undertakings that  have been given in the Crown deed by
acknowledgments and apologies are absolutely important and necessary.
Mr Horomia, being the good local MP that he is for Ikaroa-R āwhiti, raised a number
of points about sewage spewing out into th e bay and affecting the iwi and the general
population of the area. One important body that is established through this settlement is
the local leadership board. I refer him to clause 43 of the bill. The purpose of this board,
which will be made up of all the iwi in the area and also the local authorities, is to
“contribute to the sustainable management of  the natural and physic al resources in the
… area for the use and enjoyment of … fu ture generations, while recognising and
providing for the traditiona l relationship of Ngai T āmanuhiri, [and other iwi] with their
ancestral lands, water, sites, wāhi tapu” areas, and so on. I hope that that body, which is
a permanent committee and must not be di scharged without th e agreement of the
specified appointers in the council, will be able to start to address some of these matters.
Mr Horomia has very eloquently spoken this afternoon as well about the absolute need,
4054 Ngai T āmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bill 26 Jul 2012
following the passage of this legislation, for the Crown to live up to its commitments.
This is not a one-off, warm feelings situati on. This creates a new relationship, and there
are ongoing obligations that will need to be addressed. He and I have talked about ways
in which that could be done, and I very much appreciate his contribution.
This is a historic milestone for Ngai T āmanuhiri. The deed was the first settlement
agreed between the Crown and an iwi from T ūranga, where the Crown committed some
very serious Treaty breaches, and I agree with  all those speakers who have said today,
and throughout the course of the four deba tes, that it is important that people know
something about what happened. It is a sham e that the media, which are quite happy to
report the more contentious as pects of House business, have  not bothered to be here
today to listen to some of this debate, because it is very important. I acknowledge all
those officials with whom I have worked  over the years. The Office of Treaty
Settlements officials worked very hard on these matters. They are not “nine-to-fivers” at
all. In fact, I was in the office the day we in itialled the deed of settlement at about 12.30
in the morning, because Paul James, the former director, had phoned me, and wanted
me to talk to the Ngai T āmanuhiri representatives about on e or two matters. That is the
level of commitment that I have received from the Office of Treaty Settlements. I
acknowledge Mr Horomia, I acknowledge my friends in the M āori Party who have
worked so closely with me on this, and I ac knowledge my other mi nisterial colleagues.
It is a great day; a great day for Ngai T āmanuhiri. It is not the end of it. It is the
beginning of a new relationship—a very pos itive one. I salute you for all you do, and
look forward to working with you in the years to come.

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: T ēnā koe e te Kaiwhakamana,
tēnā koutou e te Whare, ia ng ā tāngata o ng ā pari e m ā rā, e Ngai T āmanuhiri, t ēnā
koutou, tēnā koutou. Nau mai, haere mai, whakatau mai ki te Pāremata e takatū nei, tēnā
koutou, tēnā tātou katoa.
[Thank you, Mr Speaker, and greetings to you, the House, and indeed those people
from yonder white cliffs, Ngai Tāmanuhiri, salutations and greetings to you collectively.
Welcome, draw closer to Parliament standing here ready, acknowledgments to you and
to us all.]
I am delighted to stand and make my cont ribution on this, the final passage of the
Ngai Tāmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bill. As a ne w member, it has been a thrill actually
being a member of the M āori Affairs Committee to follow the passage of this bill right
the way through to the House, from the firs t reading, select committee hearings, second
reading, and now to this final reading. So it is a steep learning curve for me.
Being the member for Te Tai Tonga, there is  actually a connection, in addition to the
Ngāi Tahu whakapapa connection that we share with our Tahu P ōtiki and our
whanaunga here in Ngai T āmanuhiri. There is also a common connection, because our
whanaunga there, T ūtekawa Wyllie, was also the member for Te Tai Tonga a few
elections back. So we do share many things  in common. But I am delighted to be
speaking at this stage.
We have heard this afternoon about the shared history that Ngai T āmanuhiri share
with Rongowhakaata. Therefore, the Crown’s breaches of the Treaty, its
acknowledgments, and its apologies as set ou t in this bill are very, very similar and
aligned to the same breaches that occurred  to Rongowhakaata, when I think of the
attacks at Waerenga a Hika , the loss of life at Ng ātapa, and the tensions that were over
there on Wharekauri. So you cannot  differentiate the two. The two iwi were part of all
of those atrocities, so it is appropriate that  they are acknowledged, they are recorded in
this bill, in the deed of se ttlement, and flowing through now into the passage of this
legislation.
26 Jul 2012 Ngai Tāmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bill 4055
We know that the redress that is offered, and that is part of the package that we are
putting through today, does not compensate for the loss that has been inflicted on these
iwi for many generations, but as Minister Finlayson noted, this is a step forward. This is
a beginning, and we have seen it happening right across the motu for the past 30-odd
years in terms of the modern-day Treaty settle ment process. So this is a very hallmark
occasion for Ngai Tāmanuhiri.
I have had the pleasure of working with Ngai T āmanuhiri, when I was with Ng āi
Tahu. I am thinking of a settlement in a differe nt context, and that was in the fisheries
context. I acknowledge the clos e association that Ngai T āmanuhiri has had with Ng āi
Tahu, and, in particular, the Treaty Tribes Coalition, and the support and the
whanaungatanga that I had the privilege of being amongst and working with in the years
when I was there—and it is still strong today.
There are many elements to these settlements, as my colleagues have spoken about. I
would just like to pick up on what my  matua Parekura mentioned, about how
disappointed we are in some aspects of thes e settlements. We know that the Crown has
vast assets as its disposal—all the king’ s horses and all the king’s men you can muster,
and write out a $1.7 billion cheque to bail out some investors in a failed finance
company when you really have to; when it really wants to.
I just want to say how disappointed I am in  that the arrangements in some of our
Treaty settlements could go a lot further. I look at the arrangements of Ngai Tāmanuhiri,
and it is great that we  have had the recognition of the mana of Te Kur ī a Paoa / Young
Nick’s Head, but I prefer Te Kur ī a Paoa. But for this wh ānau here to go and visit their
wāhi tapu they have to seek permission fr om the American owne r of the surrounding
adjacent lands. That is not good enough.
There are too many examples of M āori magnanimity—that is a word that my tuahine
Nanaia was speaking about this after noon. There are too many examples of
magnanimity in Treaty redresses these days. So receiving back our sacred mountains
and our islands for a period of 24 hours, and then having to re-gift them to the people of
New Zealand, smacks of paternalism and an unwillingness to fully acknowledge the
wrong. I would just like to encourage this Mini ster and in all future Treaty settlement
processes that the Crown really  does make an effort to make  sure that there is full
recognition of the mana of  the owners of those w āhi tapu sites such as Te Kur ī a Paoa,
and many others that will be coming through in  Treaty settlements that are yet to come
through this House. I would lik e to think that the Crown can  also be adventurous and
maybe look at having a chat with the American landowners, arranging a round of golf,
or having a few drinks, but coming up with a solution where everyone’s mana is
enhanced, and that the end result will be ne ver again having to ask permission to visit
Te Kurī a Paoa.
We have seen in other elements the gi fting of the right to  purchase back the
Pakowhai Scenic Reserve and other very important w āhi tapu sites. Again, it would be
good to see, in terms of future settlements,  more commitment and more going back to
the actual mana whenua and the aggrieved Treaty partner. Yes,  the acknowledgments
and the apologies are vitally important, and it would be good to see some more
measures being taken whereby some more c ontrol and rangatiratan ga can actually go
back to the mana whenua for their sacred sites.
This is a defining moment for Ngai T āmanuhiri, but also I think it is a step forward,
and we are looking at economic developmen t opportunities that wi ll flow on through
these settlements. I wish Ngai T āmanuhiri all the best in terms of their future activities
and their aspirations. I know th ey are highly skilled and a ve ry well-organised iwi, and
they have got some very talented people in their midst. I look forward to seeing what is
going to happen in the T ūranga region when we look at the likes of our recapitalised
4056 Ngai T āmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bill 26 Jul 2012
iwi: Rongowhakaata, Ngai T āmanuhiri, Mahaki to come, and also the various land
incorporation interests in that  region. I am sure that will  be a driving force for the
Tūranga region in the coming years.
This is our final bill for the day. I am delight ed that I have been able to make this
contribution right the way through the proce ss through this House. I would just like to
conclude by mihi-ing once again to the wh ānau of Ngai Tāmanuhiri who have travelled
all the way down here to support this day. I think of all the people on the claims
committees and the researchers, and a 20-ye ar process that has gone from tribunal
hearings right through negotiati ons with the Crown, all the way through to a deed of
settlement, and then a long pa ssage through the House right up to this stage here. So I
thank you. My colleague Charles mentioned the gratitude that we have for your
partnership with the Crown through this process. We are looking forward to seeing what
that future will hold beyond the passage of this  bill. So I mihi to you all. Kia ora an ō
tātou katoa.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker, t ēnā koutou te
Whare Pāremata. He mihi ki Te Wiki o Te Reo M āori, Te Reo Rangatira. He mihi nui
ki ngā iwi, hapū, whānau o Tūranga-nui-a-Kiwa, Ngai Tāmanuhiri me Rongowhakaata.
[Thank you, Mr Speaker, and salu tations to you, collectively, of Parliament House. I
applaud M āori Language Week, the Chiefly Language, and greatly appreciate the
tribes, subtribes, and families of Gisborne, Ngai Tāmanuhiri, and Rongowhakaata.]
Before I speak about the Greens’ support for the Ngai T āmanuhiri Claims Settlement
Bill I would like to address Ngai T āmanuhiri and their negotiating team in particular.
There is an English whakatauk ī “Fools rush in where angels fear to tread”, and I would
like to apply that to my second reading sp eech, which contained unmandated inferences
for which I apologise wholeheartedly. My speech stepped over the line in terms of
representation issues, and no one from Ngai T āmanuhiri asked me to do that. I therefore
express my regret and my respects to th ose of you who are here  today from Ngai
Tāmanuhiri and those who were unable to travel, who are here in spirit.
But to return to the third reading of this bi ll, which the Green Party is happy to
support, this is a significant moment in th e history of Aotearoa New Zealand. Ngai
Tāmanuhiri have travelled down the long coast to  be here, and the Green Party wants to
pay respects for the long years of waiting a nd the long years of work. After more than
100 years of marginalisation, in cluding major losses of whenua , detention without trial,
and summary executions in the 1860s, wh ich created unimaginable suffering and
ongoing poverty, there was, I believe, more th an 20 years of hard work and struggle on
this claim to reach this point, and therefor e it is time to celebrate your mahi and what
has been achieved.
My partner, Gordon Jackman, grandson of  Doris Black of Muriwai, was the
archaeologist working on a small part of the preparation for this day, and is unable to be
here, but we both feel deeply the privilege of  the opportunities of learning a little about
the history of Ngai T āmanuhiri and their rohe. The local opportunity from this
settlement is the building of stronger re lationships, the Anzac commemoration events,
and the collective work on Te Wherowhero Lagoon, which is part of this agreement.
These are foundations, and we are hopeful that P ākōwhai Scenic Reserve can also
become part of the building of those local re lationships, which make Te Tiriti a reality
not just in law but in the hearts and minds. The commitment to Ngai Tāmanuhiri having
an enhanced participation in resource manage ment processes in th eir rohe will also
benefit everyone in Te Tai Rāwhiti.
Early today the Minister for Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations spoke of the truly
unique aspect of every Treaty claim process,  and this is so powerfully true of the
matters at the heart of this bill. Part of the maunga Te Kur ī a Paoa is a reserve that is
26 Jul 2012 Ngai Tāmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bill 4057
now vested in Ngai T āmanuhiri, and named Te Kur ī a Paoa / Young Nick’s Head.
When the white sails came over the horizon and saw those white cliffs, everything
occurred from that moment and has led to th is moment and to the necessity for justice
and redress. Naming is so important, and the Green Party supports names as expressions
of dual heritage, but we belie ve that dual heritage must be fully acknowledged by both
parties, not just the iwi, for healing to really take place.
The struggles over Te Kur ī a Paoa have been long, and the Green Party wishes to
acknowledge the importance of this maunga, wh ich the late Rod D onald MP, our first
co-leader, visited in 2002 to tautoko the efforts for the maunga to be recognised as
tangata whenua land, and the first place where the cultures sighted each other. In 2002
another winter h īkoi started walking to Wellingto n, supported by some people who are
no longer with us. P ākehā and tangata Tiriti katoa have  reason to appreciate the gift
Ngai Tāmanuhiri have given the nation in thei r staunch upholding of the significance of
Te Kurī a Paoa to us all.
The redress in this agreement will also allow the implementation of some dreams and
plans regarding the Wharerata Forest and w āhi tapu, the cultural economic future of
tamariki mokopuna. Again, we all benefit from this, although, like others in the House,
the Greens would like to see a larger quantum in this agreement.
The one comment the Green Part y would add to this and to all claims is the need for
the Kāwanatanga to resource the education of P ākehā and tangata Tiriti katoa, because
our role is to make sure the wo rk done by the iwi themselves, the M āori Affairs
Committee, and the Minister is recognised and understood by all as a living history that
we are all part of, so it can reach its liber ating potential from th e grievous history of
colonisation, which Ngai Tāmanuhiri and iwi katoa have all suffered.
I would just like to finish by congratulating Ngai T āmanuhiri. The Green Party
supports your ongoing leadership and your ra ngatiratanga. Earlier today David Clendon
MP spoke about truth and reco nciliation, as well as Treat y settlement. I support his
words and those of Metiria Ture i, that this needs to happen at a local and national level
and it is time for P ākehā katoa to step up on those issues. But in the meantime, just let
me say that it has been a privilege to have  been connected in a small way with the
journey, and to have lived within your rohe . I am humbled to have met you all. Kia ora
koutou katoa.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: T ēnā koe. E ng ā reo, e ng ā
mana, e ngā hau e wh ā; ko Jonathan Young taku ingoa. T ēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, tēnā
koutou katoa.
[Greetings to you. To the languages, aut horities and four winds; my name is
Jonathan Young. Greetings, salutations, and acknowledgments to you all.]
It is my great pleasure and privilege to be  able to stand in s upport of, and speak on,
this third reading of the bill for Ngai T āmanuhiri, the Ngai T āmanuhiri Claims
Settlement Bill. Before I speak I just want  to extend the apologies of Mrs Tolley, who
cannot be here today because she is unwell.  She would love to have been here to
acknowledge this day with you.
I want to bring my thoughts round to my colleague’s comments—my colleague from
the M āori Affairs Committee—regarding Te Kur ī a Paoa slash Young Nick’s Head. I
think that was a very interesting and fort hright comment that the honourable member
Horomia brought out. We all know the Europ ean history. Nicholas Young was a sailor
on Captain’s Cook ship on his first voyage he re. He was just a young boy and he was a
stowaway on the Endeavour. He sighted Young Nick’s Head , as it was called because
of that sighting by him—but it was also called Te Kurī a Paoa—on 7 October 1769.
I remember when as a young boy we would have holidays as a family on the East
Coast, and, whether it be true or not, my mum and dad said to me that that boy, Nick
4058 Ngai T āmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bill 26 Jul 2012
Young, was one of our forebears—we cam e from the Youngs. Look, I do not know
whether it was true or not. Ma ybe it was one of those storie s that a dad told his son.
Maybe it was part of our mythology. But let me tell you how it made me feel, and how I
now understand how you feel: it made me feel important. It made me feel that this was a
place of beginning. It made me feel that here was a significant place that I had
attachment to. That is from a Pākehā. How much more, how much more, for you.
So I want to talk about the slash, because th e slash is not a cut to the heart. The slash
is the joining of peoples. It is like you would take, for example, two branches and you
would graft them together. In  order to do that, to make a living people, a living tree,
there is a slash—there is a cut. So my thought to you toda y is that I know what you are
saying, honourable member, but perhaps there is  also another way to  look at it, because
if we can resolve our past, and build our future together as New Zealanders in Aotearoa,
and have a future, and I know that the redres s never measures up to what was lost, it is
something that you can take and you can move forward with.
So it has been a long, long time, and we ha ve come to this place, come to this
afternoon. My hope and my prayer is that fr om this day forward you will find increased
strength, you will find increased resolve, and you will find increased ability to feel the
mana, to feel the location and the reconnect ion, and that you will have some economic
strength to build your future, and that together we will build this small nation into a
great nation. Tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou katoa. Kia ora.

items.speaker: BRENDAN HORAN
items.text: I would like to follow on from the comments of
all of my colleagues who have gone before me , and to say what a fantastic day today is
and how wonderful it is to be here. Earlier this morning I was leading the charge against
those people who are not here, but then I thought, well, to o bad about them, they are
missing out—they are missing out. All day amazing things have been spoken of, and
amazing people have been here. I would like to acknowledge the kaum ātua who are
here—all of you up there. I acknowledge how hard it has been for all of you to get here,
but you are here, and you made the journey.
It is hard to mention peopl e, but there are a lot of people, and I would like to say
hello to Olive and Temple Isaacs. I w ould also like to acknowledge Nolan Raih ānia
from the M āori Battalion. In 1978 I worked in Whakat āne Hospital and I had the
privilege of looking after George Raurina. George had been an interpreter with the
Māori Battalion, and I was about to embark on a trip overseas to university in Canada,
and he taught me all these different language s. His story is an amazing one. He is gone
now, but Nolan represents all of those brav e men that we lost, and how wonderful and
what a privilege it is to have you here, Nolan. Kia ora.
I would like to also follow  on from the Hon Parekura Horomia and the Hon Chris
Finlayson on the question of the sewage in  Gisborne. I love the ocean. I have been
involved in surf lifesaving, and from a very young age would always make the trek over
to Gisborne to compete, to go surfin g, or to go and plunder some of that p āua and kai
moana that was there. I have paddled out th ere and seen that sewage coming up, and it
is a disgrace. The fact that the Minister has sa id that he is prepared to look at that fills
me with joy. It can no longer be swept under the carpet, and it must go to the front of
the queue—the cleaning up of that sewage.
I would just like to speak a very small part on Ngai T āmanuhiri. This tribe is a small
one, but one of prodigious strength and mana. T āmanuhiri’s mountain or maunga, Te
Kurī a Paoa or Young Nicks Head, is there and it is there for all to see. As Parekura said
earlier, that was the first th ing Captain Cook’s crew saw wh en they visited Aotearoa. I
must say that 2019 is going to be a very in teresting year, is it  not, with the 250 th
anniversary of the sighting of your maunga by Europeans. Their waka, Horouta, rests in
the lagoon at the base of Te Kur ī a Paoa. Although the Tāmanuhiri people are relatively
26 Jul 2012 Ngai Tāmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bill 4059
small in number, they are gi ant in their connections, and they closely whakapapa into
Ngati Porou, Ngāi Tahu, Rongowhakaata, and others. Th is ability to easily and cleverly
communicate rose to the fore in negotiations. As well as their nimbleness shown in the
move to settle first of the three Tūranga groups, there is also real elegance to the level of
cultural links in the strands of the commercial redress afforded to T āmanuhiri in this
Ngai T āmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bill, with a package involving profound cultural
threads.
So congratulations to the negotiators. To t hose who have passed on but are here with
us in spirit, salutations. And to all of those who have worked so hard for a positive
outcome, thank you, thank you, and, again, thank you.
Toitū te whenua, toitū te tangata, toitū te mana—the land endures, the people prevail,
the mana is secure. Kia kaha, kia māia, kia manawanui.
[Be strong, be brave, be stout-hearted.]

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: Te mea tuatahi, kei a koutou aku rangatira, t ēnā
koutou, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou katoa. Mihi kau atu au ki te tuahine o taku hungarei e
takoto mai rā i roto i te rohe o Ngāti Porou, i te marae o Awatere. Nō reira e Mere, haere
atu rā, haere atu rā.
[The first thing is to acknowledge my leaders; greetings to you, greetings to you, and
greetings to you all. I pay a tribute to the si ster of my mother-in-law lying in state there
in the region of Ngāti Porou on the Awatere Marae. So farewell, Mary, farewell.]
I have been given the privil ege of winding up, so that so rt of cuts out what I was
going to say. I know it is a ploy by my mate ove r there, Parekura Horomia. I do want to
pay salutations not only to our brilliant Mi nister for Treaty of  Waitangi Negotiations
and the Treaty negotiations team from the Office of Treaty Settlements but also to my
colleagues on the Māori Affairs Committee, who I think have done a sterling job. I also
want to pay due respect to the Hon Parekur a Horomia, who back in the day, when he
was a wee bit younger, used to come to my office as Minister of M āori Affairs. He
would eat everything in the kitchen and leave nothing in the bar, but I tell the House and
tell the nation that you could not get a better advocate for M āori. Quite frankly, the
House has been well served by my colleague’s time in the House and his advocacy. But
we also had some discussions about how we  thought the world should run. It was just
like when my uncle used to come to our house and talk to my old man until about 4
o’clock in the morning, and they would basical ly solve the world’s problems as well. It
must be a trait of Māori to go through that as mates, as cousins, as friends, as whānau.
I am not going to dwell too much on the inner workings of the settlement in this Ngai
Tāmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bill. Suffice it to  say that this has been a momentous
day. When was the last time the nation sa w Parliament give its time over to the
settlement of Treaty agreements? When was the last time we ha d a sitting from 9
o’clock to 6 o’clock ostensibly on Treaty sett lement bills? I thought to myself, and said
to myself, earlier in the day: “Is this a good thing or is this a bad thing? Are we
ghettoising the Treaty settlements by putting them on one day, or are we giving them
their fair due?” I believe it is the latter—that we are giving part of our history, part of
our story, due recognition in the House of Parliament.
And actually it is not the House of Parlia ment; it is the House of Representatives.
That basically means to me that it is the House that is our vis itors’ House—it is the
House of Representatives. It is the House where we stand and deliv er on all manner of
things in a representative role for the people outside. It is a wonderful, wonderful day to
have you all here, especially, I suppose, knowing where T āmanuhiri is as well. It was
only very recently that I got to stand on the shores of Muriwai, contemplating my career
in politics, and whether it was, maybe, going to go for another 3 years, or maybe end
abruptly. I was lucky. It went on for another—well, it is going on for another 3 years.
4060 Ngai T āmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bill 26 Jul 2012
I have said for the last 2 weeks that this is all about the tapestry, the brilliant tapestry
of New Zealand’s history, and I do echo what the Hon Parekura Horomia says about the
naming, what it actually means, and wher e it lies in the hearts of the hau k āinga, the
home people. But I also feel for my mate w ho was sitting here, who is related to those
Youngs, and to Nicholas Young. As for whether th at is true or not, I mean, like he says,
I think it is a good story and I will be telling that story around the nation as well—that
Young Nick’s Head was named after his tupuna. Like I said, whether it  is true or not,
most of us know—most M āori know—of its true name, its real name, and pay due
respects.

items.speaker: Here is something else to ponder
items.text: regardless  of whether land is given back, returned,
or whatever, when we drive past it, even if it does not belong to us any more, we still
say “See that piece of land over there? That’s ours.” I think that is a good thing. I think
that if we can pay due recognition, and if we can pay what we owe in the final analysis,
that is a great thing for this  history, and other nations ar ound the world can have a look
at us. I want to take that and refer to the Black Hills of Dakota, where in the 1860s there
was a treaty between the in digenous people and the Govern ment of the USA, stating
that they would have tino rangatiratanga ove r this block of land, the Black Hills of
Dakota. They signed the treaty, and one da y somebody found gold and that was it. And,
you know, for ever and a day, it even went as high as the Supreme Court to say how the
treaty was broken.
The agreement that T āmanuhiri has is with the Crow n. Make no mistake: every one
of us sitting here today is the Crown. It is not just the Government; it is the Opposition
as well—those people are the Crown. My a dvice throughout the debate has been to
watch out for the hawkers and the shysters, but also to watch out  for the Crown. Watch
out for the Government, because in its wish to  take the country forward it might slip up
now and then, or it might tr ip over now and then. It is  a good idea just to keep a
watching brief on what we do as the Crown. So that is another piece of advice.
I will not go on too much longer, other than to say: ng ā mihi nunui ki a koutou katoa
ngā uri o ngā aitua o Ngai Tāmanuhiri. Tino hari taku ngākau i kite au i a koutou i roto i
tōku nei Whare, i t ō Whare, n ō reira, t ēnā koutou, t ēnā koutou. Kua pai t ā koutou
haerenga ki te hau kāinga a muri i tēnei kōrero, nō reira, ngā manaakitanga, ngā aroha ki
a koutou katoa, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, kia ora mai tātou katoa.
[I acknowledge you greatly , descendants of Ngai T āmanuhiri disasters. I am
particularly pleased to see you here in my  House, your House, so greetings and
salutations to you collectively. All will be  well for your return home following this
address, so blessings and compassion to you all, greeting, greetings, and greetings to us
all.]
Bill read a third time.
Waiata
The House adjourned at 6.06 p.m.

26 Jul 2012 Business Statement 4009 
THURSDAY, 26 JULY 2012 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Karakia. 
BUSINESS STATEMENT 
Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON (Minister for Treaty of Waitangi 
Negotiations) on behalf of the Leader of the House: In the absence of both the Leader 
of the House and the Deputy Leader of the Ho use, I am required to read this statement 
to the House. I do apologise. I have not had time to memorise it. When the House 
resumes on Tuesday, 31 July—[ Interruption] never call me petulant—the Government 
will look to progress the Committee stage of  the Biosecurity Law Reform Bill, the 
Juries (Jury Service and Protec tion of Particulars of Jury List Information) Amendment 
Bill, the Commerce Commission (Internatio nal Co-operation, and Fees) Bill, the 
Sentencing (Aggravating Factors) Amen dment Bill, and the Appropriation (2012/13 
Estimates) Bill. 
Mr SPEAKER : I call the honourable shadow Lead er of the House, who will not 
need to read it at all. 
Hon TREVOR MALLARD (Labour—Hutt South) : In the absence of my friend 
and colleague Russel Norman, I will not read a response. 
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Infrastructure Investment Programme—Progress 
1. Dr CAM CALDER (National)  to the Minister of Finance: What progress is the 
Government making with its multi-billion dollar infrastructure programme? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Finance) : Our progress on infrastructure is 
good. We have invested $5 billion in infras tructure such as schools, broadband, and 
hospitals over the last four Budgets, and billions more upgrading our State highway 
networks and the national grid. The first road of national significance project, Victoria 
Park Tunnel, has been completed and th ere is good progress on the rest. We have 
upgraded on average over 16,000 State houses  a year since 2009, a nd are on track to 
insulate every State house built before 1978 by the end of the year. Of course, we have 
put aside $5.5 billion to help fund the rebuild of Christchurch infrastructure, which is 
getting under way. 
Dr Cam Calder: What steps has the Government ta ken to improve the quality of its 
infrastructure investment? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : Well, that is a good question, because just having more 
infrastructure is one aspect of it, but having high-quality infrastructure is, in the long 
run, more important. We have improved the way the Government makes its own plans 
and the way it gets consents and finances its infrastructure through the reform of the 
Resource Management Act, setting up the Na tional Infrastructure Unit, and setting up 
the Environmental Protection Authority. This has introduced more discipline into the 
Government process. Last year we issued  the second National Infrastructure Plan, 
which shows that our infrastr ucture is generally improving, but it does highlight those 
areas where we need to do a better job.  
Dr Cam Calder: How will the Government fund its large infrastructure investment? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : The planned investment over th e next 4 years is large, at 
around $17 billion. This will be paid for thr ough a mixture of funding sources. Some of 
it, of course, will come from petrol tax and road-user charges on the roads, some will 
4010 Questions for Oral Answer 26 Jul 2012 
come from depreciation, and a considerable amount will come from direct funding from 
the Government. The direct funding from the Government will be channelled through 
the Future Investment Fund, which was set up to  take the proceeds of the partial share 
sales and invest those in future publicly owned infrastructure. Treasury is forecasting 
sale proceeds of $5 billion to $7 billion over th e next 3 to 5 years, and this will assist 
with a $17 billion infrastructure investment programme.  
Hon David Parker : Does he agree with the 52 percent of business leaders in the 
New Zealand Herald ’s “Mood of the Boardroom” survey that other than returning to 
surplus, the Government has no adequate pl an to encourage the economic growth and 
jobs needed to stop so many young New Zealanders moving to Australia? 
Hon Steven Joyce : Oh, so not enough plans today? So we have changed from too 
many plans again.  
Hon BILL ENGLISH: No, I do not, and as my colleague Steven Joyce has pointed 
out, the Labour Party cannot decide—on some days there are too many plans, and on 
the other days there is no plan. We have outlined the programme, outlined the plan, 
including to the “Mood of the Boardroom” se ssion this morning. I can tell the member 
that it has pretty broad support among the business community.  
Overseas Investment Rules—2010 Sale of Crafar Farms to Natural Dairy 
2. RICHARD PROSSER (NZ First)  to the Minister for Land Information : Can 
the public have confidence that the Overseas Investment Office is taking prompt action 
in relation to all breaches of the Overseas Investment Act 2005; if so, how? 
Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON (Actin g Minister for Land Information) : 
Yes. The Overseas Investment Office promp tly investigates all suspected breaches of 
the Overseas Investment Act 2005. I have some good news for that honourable member: 
in the period 1 July 2011 to 30 June 2012, 100 percent—100 percen t—of public alerts 
about potential breaches were  assessed for possible invest igation within 10 working 
days.  
Richard Prosser: Given that answer, will he tell the House what action the Overseas 
Investment Office has taken in respect of th e four Crafar farms sold to an overseas 
investor without consent; or, alternatively, will he explain why no action has been 
taken? 
Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON : I do not have particular information about 
particular applications or particular concerns to hand. If the member wants an answer to 
a particular question, I suggest he either ask it as the primar y question or put it down as 
a written question to the Minister.  
Richard Prosser: How can the public have confidence in the Overseas Investment 
Office when UBNZ Assets Holdings, a co mpany associated with May Wang, who 
failed a good-character test, was able to pur chase four of the Crafar farms without 
permission and get away with it? 
Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON : The same principle applies: if the member 
wants direct answers to speci fic questions, he should eith er ask them as a primary 
question or put them down as a written question.  
Brendan Horan : I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Did we not determine a 
number of weeks ago that if  a Minister did not know the answer, the Minister should 
simply say that they do not know the answer? 
Mr SPEAKER : Well, I think the Minister basically said that, but he was a little 
more helpful in suggesting that maybe if  members want detailed information in 
answers, they need to make it clear in th e primary question what they are asking. I do 
not think the Minister was being unhelpful. 
26 Jul 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 4011 
New Zealand - Australia Migration—18 to 30 Age Range 
3. Hon DAVID PARKER (Labour)  to the Minister of Finance: Does he stand by 
his statement regarding migration to Austra lia “What’s the point of standing in the 
airport crying about it?”; if so, how many of the 53,763 people that migrated to 
Australia in the year to June 2012 are from 18 to 30 years of age in number and 
percentage terms? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Finance) : Yes; and, as I said in the rest of that 
statement, we have just got to compete. New Zealand should show the aspiration and 
confidence that it can compete with a la rger, more wealthy economy for our young

One hundred and twenty years ago in Apr il 1893, Te Kooti Rikirangi uttered these 
unforgettable words: “Ko te waka he hoehoenga mō koutou i muri i ahau nā te ture tērā. 
Mā te ture an ō te ture e aki. The canoe that you mu st paddle when I am gone is that of

fruition. The Rongowhakaata Claims Settlement Bill will finally settle the historical 
Treaty of Waitangi claims of Rongowhakaata.  
The settlement journey for Rongowhakaata and Ng ā Uri o Te Kooti Rikirangi has 
been a long one. Many who have borne the weight  of this journey are no longer with us 
today, and we acknowledge and remember them. The Waitangi Tribunal’s 2004 report 
concluded that T ūranga’s history includes some of the darkest and most dramatic 
moments in our nation’s history. The tri bunal described the breaches arising from 
Crown military action against the iwi as some of the worst in New Zealand. But it went 
further and laid a challenge th at I believe it is incumbent on all of us to pick up. The 
tribunal noted that it could not help but think that the unsettled state of relations 
between Māori and P ākehā is in part due to the fact that these stories are remembered 
only by tangata whenua and a few specialist historians. This leaves the nation in an 
unenviable state of flux, a nd I quote from the 2004 repo rt: “While only one side 
remembers the suffering of the past, dialogue will always be difficult. One side 
commences the dialogue with anger and the other side has no idea why. Reconciliation 
cannot be achieved by this means.” How do we avoid repeating the mistakes of the 
past? What price is paid for the oppressive policies and injustices suffered in the name 
of the law?  
This settlement records the Crown’s d eep remorse over wrongs done. The apology 
expresses profound regret that  over the generations to th e present day Crown actions

have significantly impacted on Rongowhakaat a’s social and trad itional structures, 
autonomy, and ability to exercise customary rights and responsibilities. The apology is a 
sincere attempt to report the Crown’s failure since 1840 to respect the mana of 
Rongowhakaata and their rangatir atanga. It is difficult for a nyone outside of this iwi to 
truly appreciate the depth of  loss and prejudice that has been suffered. The words of a 
young 17-year-old give voice to that grief,  which has endured over generations. W ētini 
Wilkins-Larkin, a direct descendant of Te K ooti Rikirangi, told the story of his nannies, 
Hine Campbell and Mihi Larkin. “This str uggle”—he said—“goes back in history, to 
the time even when my grandmother wa s a young school girl who experienced the 
stigma and shame of being a direct des cendant of the koroua. I’m told that the 
Matawhero massacre would be a common topic in the school curriculum, and that my 
Nan would often be a scapegoat for other pupi ls, that the finger was pointed to her in 
disgust and that she would even hide under the shadow of her desk, with her face hidden 
behind her hands.” What a painful memory to live with throughout your life. How do 
Ngā Uri o Te Kooti Rikirangi move past the stigmatisation of Te Kooti and his 
descendants? It will take time, and our greates t hope is that in the course of the journey 
we witness today, we will reach a time when all New Zealanders look on Te Kooti as 
the founder of Te Haahi Ringat ū, acknowledge his inspirational leadership, and 
appreciate his commitment to the preservation of Te Reo me ōna tikanga, just as his 
followers from my own iwi continue to follow and believe today.  
This bill expresses that recognition and redress for the bitter grievances of 
Rongowhakaata that are long overdue. That recognition includes knowledge that the 
Crown used force in T ūranga in November 1865 when there was absolutely no need to 
do so. The Crown’s attack on Waerenga a Hika, whose occupants included women and 
children, was unwarranted and unj ust and caused severe and l ong-term prejudice to this 
iwi. The summary executions at Ng ātapa by Crown forces in 1869 tarnished the honour 
of the Crown and will live on in the hear ts and minds of Rongowhakaata descendants, 
their w’ ānau, and their hap ū. The indefinite detention in harsh conditions on the 
Chatham Islands without trial or the laying of charges was an injustice depriving 
Rongowhakaata of their basic human rights. The enduring cruelty of Crown actions was 
epitomised in the 1869 deed of cession, resultin g in the extinguishment of all of their 
customary land interests. In effect, the Crown confiscated Rongowhakaata land, 
including interests in over 50,000 acres at Patutahi, and by exclusion from titles 
awarded by the Poverty Bay Commission.  
On days like this it is unimaginable,  the sadness deep w ithin the soul of 
Rongowhakaata, nor can the ongoing feelings about the Crown actions be put into 
words. 
The illegal imprisonment of a quarter of the adult male population of T ūranga on 
Wharekauri, and the loss in the war of an estimated 43 percent of  their adult male 
population, including the illegal execution of a third to a half of that number, were 
described by the tribunal as a “stain on our  national history and character”. The final 
chapter in the tribunal’s report, “Hei Whak amahutanga: The Healing” Is headed with 
these words: “Whakamoea nga patu ki nga patu rakau, kia whanau ko te pai. Put to 
sleep the evil words and weapons of war so that goodness can prevail.”  
One of the ways in which resolution may be achieved is in addressing the 
confiscation of Te Hau ki T ūranga, the elaborate w’are whakairo carved by the expert 
carver Raharuhi Rukupō of Ngāti Kaipoho. Crown troops took possession of Te Hau in 
1867 in the aftermath of Waerenga a Hika. The acquisition of this cherished tribal 
whare, which is held by Te Papa here in Wellington, has been a source of great pain to 
this iwi, and it is right that redress relating to  Te Hau lies at the heart of this settlement. 
The settlement legislation contains within it the vesting in Rongow hakaata of sites of

 In the years 1840 to 1860 Rongowhakaata en joyed a period of peace and economic 
development. With the local rivers, fertile soil, and kai moana, Rongowhakaata lived in 
abundance, enjoying a measure of prosperity and of trade, and operating several trading 
ships. When approached to sell land, they  refused these things and hung on to all of 
their rawa, and their lands, and their mana. They refused to sell. What a change was 
about to take place in the next decade. 
In November 1865 large Crown military forces came to T ūranga, after fighting 
Paimarire converts on the East Coast. Th e Crown laid siege to the defensive p ā of 
Waerenga a hika, and captured  it in November 1865. At le ast 71 occupants of the p ā 
were killed during that assault. The Crow n acknowledges that it used military force 
when there was no need to do so, that it  did not pursue all reasonable options for 
preserving peace in T ūranga, and that the Crown’s att ack was unwarranted and unjust, 
and caused severe and long-term prejudice to Rongowhakaata. 
In 1866 the Crown exiled approximately 116 T ūranga men, including Te Kooti 
Rikirangi, to the Chatham Islands and we have heard k ōrero about that. They were 
detained without trial or conviction for 2 y ears, in harsh conditions, until they escaped 
in 1868. The Crown acknowledges that th e indefinite detention of many 
Rongowhakaata, including Te Kooti Rikirangi, on the Chatham Islands was an injustice 
that deprived them of basic human rights. It  was wrongful, contrary to natural justice, 
and impacted not only on the prisoners but on their wh ānau and hap ū who remained in 
Tūranga. The Crown also acknowledges that th e unjust treatment of Te Kooti Rikirangi 
4038 Rongowhakaata Claims Se ttlement Bill 26 Jul 2012 
gave him reason to distrust the Crown when he was offered the chance to return to 
Tūranga after his arrival back on the Mainland. 
But in 1868 Rongowhakaata were pressured by  the Crown to cede all their lands to 
the Crown. This cessation was made under du ress, as the Crown had threatened to 
remove all its protection unless the entir e district was ceded. All Rongowhakaata’s 
customary interests in their lands were extinguished. By December 1868 Te Kooti 
Rikirangi and his followers had retreated to Ngātapa Pā, where they were surrounded by 
Crown forces in conjunction with M āori allies. Te Kooti Riki rangi and some of his 
followers escaped in early Ja nuary 1869 and were pursued for several days. The Crown 
again acknowledges that the Ng ātapa siege and its aftermat h caused the death of many 
Rongowhakaata and had a devastating im pact on the iwi a nd the whole of T ūranga. In 
subsequent years the Poverty Bay Comm ission and the Native Land Court awarded 
individual titles, which only helped the alienation of those titles. 
These and other breaches have left Rongow hakaata virtually landless and without 
enough resources to meet their present and fu ture needs. The breaches of the Treaty in 
the T ūranga area were extremel y significant and have had many lasting effects for 
Rongowhakaata, so I would like to take this opportunity to highlight the Crown apology 
contained in the deed of settlement and,  subsequently, this Rongowhakaata Claims 
Settlement Bill. The apology is significant as it takes a step towards healing the hurt that 
is felt as a result of the Treaty br eaches. I would like to refer to t ērā whare rongonui, 
ātaahua, kua hangaia i ra ro i a Raharuhi Rukup ō, n ā, ē whakaae ana kia whakahokia 
tēnei taonga ki te iwi [ that famous and beautiful house built under the guidance of 
Raharuhi Rukupō, and I concur that this treasure be returned to the tribe]. 
But as with many Treaty settlement redress it ems, there are costs associated with the 
return of wāhi tapu or taonga. I am heartened to know that Rongowhakaata do not wish 
the return of Te Hau ki T ūranga to create a financial bur den for future generations. As 
such, Te Papa Tongarewa will work with R ongowhakaata and the Ministry for Culture 
and Heritage to ensure a sustainable future fo r the whare, particularly in relation to its 
relocation. This is a significant step towa rds righting the wrongs of the past and 
mending the relationship between Rongowhakaata and the Crown. 
This bill today also outlines  the redress provided to Ng ā Uri o Te Kooti Rikirangi, 
the other claim that we are hearing as well, and I acknowledge  Peter and Maever 
Moeau. It acknowledges and is in recognition of the stigmatisation of the descendants of 
Te Kooti Rikirangi. This redress includes the vesting of Matawhero Reserve, the 
payment of $250,000 for purposes of Te Whare R ākei o Te Kooti Rikirangi, the 
payment of $200,000 to Ng ā Uri o Te Kooti Rikirangi, and a relationship with the 
Department of Conservation with regard to interpretation material that refers to Te 
Kooti Rikirangi. This redress is a significant step towards rehabilitating the reputation 
of Te Kooti Rikirangi and acknowledgi ng the discrimination experienced by his 
descendants. 
The settlement also provides for the establishment of a central leadership group and a 
local leadership body. The centr al leadership group has been  established to provide a 
forum for Rongowhakaata,  along with other T ūranga iwi—and I think this is pretty 
important—to engage with central governme nt departments and ensure that the 
principles of the Treaty of Waitangi are being implemented in a coordinated manner 
within the Tūranga region. The local leadership body will work with the local council to 
contribute to the sustainable management of resources within the Tūranga region. These 
redress items provide Rongowha kaata with a valuable oppor tunity to engage with 
central and local government on a range of issu es that affect their rohe in the wider 
region.

Hon TARIANA TURIA (Minister for Whānau Ora) on behalf of the Minister for 
Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations : I move, That the Ngai T āmanuhiri Claims 
Settlement Bill be now read a third time . E rau rangatira m ā, tēnei te mi’i ki a koutou i 
runga i te kaupapa o te r ā. Tēnā koutou ng ā rangatira o Ngai T āmanuhiri, kātahi anō te

[I greet you, leaders of a hundredfold, in respect of the matter of the day. Salutations 
to you, the leaders of Ngai T āmanuhiri. This Parliament House has at last celebrated 
this bill, which I deem it an honour to speak to in this, its final reading. 
Acknowledgments, salutations, and congratulations to you all.]  
The Ngai T āmanuhiri Claims Settlement Bill will settle finally the historical Treaty 
of Waitangi claims of Ngai T āmanuhiri. The third reading of this bill brings to an end a 
day of great sadness and loss as the enduring memories of descendants have resonated 
throughout this Chamber. We have wept w ith them as we have traversed over the 
history we share. The loss extends beyond th e tribal boundaries to also reflect on the 
health of our nationhood. The settlement stories have impacted on the rule of law, the 
definition of just and good settlement, and the protection of M āori mana motuhake. In 
all these principles and the failures of the Cr own to live up to that ideal, it goes to the 
surface of our capacity to live up to the prom ise of the Treaty. These settlement bills, 
therefore, become a benchmark for all New Zealanders to assess the progress that we 
have achieved since the signing of Te Tiriti o Waitangi in 1840.  
Ngai Tāmanuhiri’s settlement part stretches back 20 years. Today those in the public 
gallery and all of us below reflect on those who are not with us, those who have worked 
tirelessly on Ngai T āmanuhiri’s claims and who are not here to witness this day. The 
rohe that forms the home of Ngai T āmanuhiri extends from K ōpututea, down the 
coastline over Wharerata Forest to Parit ū, and from Parit ū the area extends inland 
towards Lake Waikaremoana. It  is a beautiful pa rt of the world, an exquisite tribal 
sanctuary.  
Up until 1865 Ngai T āmanuhiri had full control of th eir lands and resources. The 
people were participating su ccessfully in the New Zeal and economy and, indeed, the 
sun shone brightly for the people of this eastern coast. When war broke out in other 
regions Ngai Tāmanuhiri remained neutral, including when fighting came close to home 
in 1865. Into this peaceful haven, then, the Crown’s attack on Waerenga a Hika is 
inexplicable. There was no need to use military force in T ūranga. The military forces 
took part in indiscriminate looting. Those attacks contribut ed to acute food shortages, 
which in themselves caused loss of life. On top of that, the dete ntion of some Ngai 
Tāmanuhiri on Wharekauri inflicted unwarranted hardship on them and their w’anau. It 
was wrongful, it was unwarranted, it was unjust, it was a breach of natural justice, and it 
was a breach of Te Tiriti o Waitangi. Well over a century later, in 1992, Eric John Tūpai 
Ruru, Tūtekawa Wyllie, and Peter Gordon lodged a claim with the Waitangi Tribunal 
on behalf of Te Aitanga-a-M āhaki, Ngai T āmanuhiri, and Rongowha kaata, referred to 
as Wai 283.  
The Minister in an earlier speech referred to settlements as going to the very heart of 
our nation, and it is in the process of telli ng our stories, documenting our truths, and 
outlining our experience that we come anywhe re close to the prospect of reconciliation. 
The Crown’s relation with Ngai T āmanuhiri has involved some of the darkest episodes

in the country’s history, and that sense of grief and loss su ffered by, and the impact on,

traditional tribal structures. As a direct consequence Ngai T āmanuhiri have lived with 
poorer housing, lower educationa l achievements, and worse h ealth than any other New 
Zealanders, yet, despite this painful history, they have made a significant contribution to 
the wealth and development of the nation, and have at all times graciously honoured 
their Treaty obligations and responsibilities.  
In particular, the settlement pays tribute to Ngai T āmanuhiri’s contribution to the 
defence of the nation. Knowing even as little as we do of the injustices that this iwi have 
suffered at the hands of the Crown, we cannot help but be overwhelmed by the spirit of 
generosity that they have shown the nation in having faith in wo rking with the Crown 
on this settlement.  
I want to be very clear for the record th at in this settlement today, the Crown is 
deeply sorry that it has failed until now to address the injustices in an appropriate 
manner. The Crown sincerely apologises fo r its many failures to respect Ngai 
Tāmanuhiri mana and to protect them fr om being left virtually landless and 
economically marginalised. We all hope that  this settlement will provide a foundation 
for this tribe and the Crown to move forward in a spirit of coopera tion, mutual benefit, 
and trust.

who lost their lives at the ha nds of the Crown. It will provide a sombre reminder to all

breaches of the Treaty of Waitangi, offers an apology, and there are various forms of 
redress, which Mrs Turia has mentioned and I am not going to repeat them in my 
speech. But this day has indeed been a long time coming. The claims were first made to 
the Waitangi Tribunal 20 years ago, in 1992. The claims were inquired into by the 
tribunal, and it reported in 2004. It is well established that the grievances that it found, 
the breaches of the Treaty, were  very serious indeed. Ngai T āmanuhiri entered

settlement, the journey is sometimes very long, because in the deed of settlement all the 
details have to be finalised, whereas in the agreement in principle, it can be a fairly

acknowledgement and the apology. One was awar e that it was a very eerie sort of
